# kuna option catalog

**Generated** by `kuna catalog --markdown` from `settableTable` in `decompiler/crates/kuna-decomp/phases.toml` -- do not edit by hand; edit the registry row and regenerate.

Set any option per run: `kuna decompile <bin> <fn> --option <name> <value>` (repeatable), `kuna decompile-all <bin> --option <name> <value>`, or the console `option <name> <value>`. Defaults are the shipped values; what a default does is described in its row below. The algorithms behind these options are described in `docs/spec/`.

Three tiers:

- **Toggleable transforms** -- restructure, duplicate, remove, or insert code; near-always better on the right source shape and wrong on the wrong one. **This is the on/off control surface.**
- **Analysis & loader passes** -- what gets discovered/decoded/named before decompilation.
- **Core rendering defaults** -- near-always-better rendering/naming/peepholes; part of the decompiler, not the control surface. Flip only for upstream byte-parity or unusual consumers.

## Toggleable transforms

The control surface: each of these can make output worse on the wrong source shape, so each stays flippable.

### `structdefs` -- on | off, default `off`

- **Symptoms:** the signature says FILE * or struct_0 * and nothing says what the fields are; a field access like f->_flags with no layout anywhere in the output; you have to run decompile-project just to read the .h for one function's struct; a synthesized struct_N appears in a parameter type with no definition.
- **What it does:** Print the definitions of the composite, enum and typedef types a function's C names ABOVE the function. kuna recovers a layout and then does not show it: a body that reads `f->_flags` names `FILE` in its signature and nothing on the surface says what a `FILE` is, so the struct the decompiler recovered is invisible to the one surface an agent reads. The renderer has existed since `kuna decompile-project` -- `PrintC::doc_type_definitions` writes every user-defined type into the export's `.h` -- but nothing called it for a single function. When on, `kuna_structdefs::referenced_types` collects the function's semantic type surface (the prototype's return and parameter types, every Varnode data-type, every mapped Symbol type behind a HighVariable), descends through typedef bases and component types -- a pointer's pointee, an array's element, a struct's fields -- and pushes each definable type in postorder, so the list is definition-before-use over exactly the referenced subset rather than the whole factory. Those roots are a superset of the type names the printer can spell (a declaration is read off a high or its symbol, the signature off the prototype, a cast off the Varnode type it casts to), so the preamble cannot miss a definition the body refers to -- and it catches the struct behind `p->field_0x8`, whose tag name the C never prints at all. The text is the SAME `render_type_definitions` the `.h` type block is built with: the forward-declaration block, then bodies, an incomplete struct printing as `typedef struct FILE FILE; /* opaque */`, core types never. A `kuna decompile-project` export's bodies suppress the preamble, because they include the header that already carries it. `kuna decompile-all --json` carries the same set as an additive per-function `types` array (name, definition text, size) so a consumer reads the layout without parsing C.
- **When to flip:** Flip on when you are reading a function whose arguments are pointers to composites and want the layout in front of you -- `structsynth`'s synthesized `struct_N`, a DWARF struct on an unstripped binary, `libctypes`' opaque `FILE`/`DIR` shells -- instead of opening the `decompile-project` header to find it. Default OFF: it is a presentation default, and a preamble in front of every function is noise for a caller diffing bodies or feeding one function to a matcher. It changes nothing but the text above the function -- the body, its line contents and every recovered type are identical either way -- but it DOES move line numbers, so a consumer pinning a line number should read `line_mappings` rather than assume the first line is the signature. The preamble is documentation, not a compilable unit: a padding member spelled `undefined1` needs the export's recompile prelude to compile, which is one more reason the project surface keeps the definitions in the header.
- **Where / provenance:** P9/type-definition-preamble · angr · presentation-default · kuna-structdefs
- **Example:** `option structdefs on`

### `devectorize` -- on | off, default `off`

- **Symptoms:** a loop summing an array prints as eight lane accumulators added into one total after the loop; a vectorised reduction is followed by a second copy of the loop over the remainder; an array sum is guarded by if (8 <= length) with a stride-eight do-while behind it; a line like v8 + v12 + v6 + v10 + v7 + v11 + v5 + v9 follows a loop.
- **What it does:** Re-roll a vectorized integer reduction into the scalar loop it came from. clang and gcc turn `for (i) sum += a[i]` into a guard `length >= S`, a stride-S loop with one accumulator per lane, a horizontal fold, an early return when `length & -S == length`, and a scalar copy of the loop that finishes the remainder or, when the guard failed, runs from zero. The pass proves the whole shape on SSA -- zero inits; lanes that zero-extend disjoint E-byte slices of loads at base + i*E + c and tile exactly S elements, for a power-of-two S the guard bounds; a fold that adds every accumulator once; both exits handing back their sums; no side effects in the arm and no global store in the arm, the remainder loop, the else block or either exit; lanes inside the bytes of their load; a guard bound that a signed compare against a negative constant does not fake; nothing defined in the arm read outside except through the phis the edge removal patches -- and removes the guard's vector edge (Funcdata::remove_branch), leaving the arm to the unreachable-block collector. Integer addition is associative and commutative modulo 2^(8Z), so the scalar loop from zero computes the same value on every input. Needs wideslice to have reduced the lanes to byte reads first; floats, saturating and sign-extended lanes are not matched.
- **When to flip:** Turn ON when an -O2/-O3 loop that sums the elements of an array comes out as a guard `if (8 <= length)`, a do-while adding `v2 & 0xff`, `v2 >> 8 & 0xff`, ... into eight separate accumulators, a line summing those accumulators, and a second do-while over `bytes[v4]` for the remainder -- and you want the source loop `v1 += bytes[v2]` instead. OFF (the default) keeps the compiler's shape, which shows the stride, the alignment of the handoff and the duplicated body. Inert on a function with no loop of that shape.
- **Where / provenance:** P3/simplification-quiescence · kuna · structure-recovery · wide-ssa-slices
- **Example:** `option devectorize on`

### `strlenscan` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** a do/while that decrements a 0xffffffffffffffff counter while stepping a char pointer until the byte read is zero; if (!v3) break; v3 -= 1; inside a loop that reads one byte per step; ~v3 - 1 or ~v3 - 5 where the source computes a string length; repnz scasb in the disassembly where IDA prints strlen.
- **What it does:** Print an inline `repnz scasb` string length as `strlen(s)`. gcc up to version 9 (at -O1 and above) and older MSVC expand `strlen` inline as `or rcx,-1; xor eax,eax; repnz scasb; not rcx` (ECX on 32-bit x86), and SLEIGH lifts the repeat prefix as a loop inside the one instruction, so the C shows `do { if (!n) break; n -= 1; ... } while (c);` over the string and `~n - 1` wherever the length is used. When on, `kuna_strlenscan` matches the two blocks the instruction lifts to on SSA, after mainloop has settled the count and the byte searched for, and proves the loop is a string length: the count enters as the all-ones constant of its width and the head leaves exactly when it is zero; the body steps the count down and the pointer up by one, reads one byte through the pointer, computes nothing else with side effects, and loops exactly while that byte is not zero (checked for all 256 values, which proves the byte searched for is zero); nothing after the loop reads the count except through a bitwise NOT. It then places `len = strlen(s)` (a typed builtin user-op, `char *` in, unsigned out) in the body, gives every value the loop hands on its final-iteration value (count `~(len + 1)`, pointer `s + len + 1`, the terminator byte zero, from which the flags follow), and removes the never-taken zero-count exit and the back edge, every scan of a function in one pass. The builtin keeps the call flag, so it is ordered like a call: a `strlen` stays where its scan was, ahead of a store, call or `free` that follows, and is never duplicated into several readers or merged across a join. A scan for another byte, one whose raw count is read, one counting from another start and one stepping backward keep their loops. Over 8 stripped decbench binaries (gcc 11, which no longer emits the idiom) the output is byte-identical; over 29 Ubuntu 20.04 gcc 9 binaries (bash, coreutils, util-linux, shadow, binutils and others) under `--mode aggressive`, 52 of 11,000 functions change, each gaining `strlen` (132 more), with 136 fewer scan loops, 1,212 fewer lines (34,588 -> 33,376) and 10 fewer gotos; 0/675 datatest assertions move.
- **When to flip:** On by default: a string length gcc 9 or older MSVC computed with `repnz scasb` reads `strlen(s)`, taken where the scan was (`v1 = strlen(s);` when it is read twice or before a store). Set it off to see the scan loop SLEIGH lifts the instruction to, as upstream prints it.
- **Where / provenance:** P3/simplification-quiescence · ida · presentation-default · kuna-strlenscan
- **Example:** `option strlenscan off`

### `rodatastring` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** stack string initialisation renders as an array-typed cast such as (char[8])s_addr._0_8_; partial-symbol slice assignments like buf._0_9_ = s_addr._16_9_ instead of the string; a recognized rodata literal never appears in the function that copies it onto the stack; builtin_strncpy call where the individual slice assignments are wanted (flip off).
- **What it does:** Collapse a read-only string block copy (wide rodata loads re-stored into the frame) into a single builtin_strncpy.
- **When to flip:** Flip off to keep the raw partial-symbol slice assignments; on (default) recovers the literal the copy spells.
- **Where / provenance:** P5/constsequence · kuna · correctness-fix · repipe-68149b8a-stack-string-invalid-cast
- **Example:** `option rodatastring off`

### `memsetrecover` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** long run of per-element constant stores instead of a single memset; unrolled or SIMD zeroing rendered as dozens of assignments; builtin_memset call where the individual element stores are wanted (flip off).
- **What it does:** Collapse a run of constant-fill stores (incl. inlined/SIMD bzero) into a single builtin_memset.
- **When to flip:** Flip off only to see the individual element stores; on (default) reconstructs the memset.
- **Where / provenance:** P5/constsequence · ghidra-upstream · correctness-fix · GH-9230/1537
- **Example:** `option memsetrecover off`

### `returnpair` -- pair | single, default `pair` (destructive opt-in)

- **Symptoms:** spurious CONCAT44 return value in a void or single-register function; two return registers joined into one double-width return (e.g. sparc o0/o1); return type twice the natural width built from a register concat.
- **What it does:** Whether a passively-active second return register may be joined into a wide return (pair) or dropped (single).
- **When to flip:** Set single PER FUNCTION when a void/single-register function shows a spurious CONCAT44 return (e.g. SPARC); DESTRUCTIVE as a global default (truncates real multi-register returns).
- **Where / provenance:** P4/trial-budget · ghidra-upstream · opt-in-tool · GH-6990
- **Example:** `option returnpair single`

### `v850indirectbranch` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** v850 jmp [reg] rendered as an indirect call instead of a recovered switch; jump table on v850 never recovered because the dispatch decodes as a computed call.
- **What it does:** On V850, reclassify a `jmp [reg]` CALLIND to BRANCHIND so switch-table recovery runs.
- **When to flip:** On by default: a V850 compiler switch dispatch through `jmp [reg]` recovers as a jump-table switch instead of a computed call. Gated on the V850 language id, so a register-indirect call on any other processor is left alone. Flip off to keep the SLEIGH lifting as a call.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/flow-classification · ghidra-upstream · opt-in-tool · GH-8817
- **Example:** `option v850indirectbranch on`

### `cortexmpriv` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** an `if (isCurrentModePrivileged())` block wraps every interrupt-mask or special-register access in Cortex-M firmware; `isCurrentModePrivileged()` appears in the emitted C at all; a Cortex-M function has more basic blocks and branches than its source; `getBasePriority()`/`isIRQinterruptsEnabled()`/`getCurrentExceptionNumber()` are each read under their own conditional.
- **What it does:** On ARM Cortex-M firmware, assume the core is privileged, so the `isCurrentModePrivileged()` guard the vendored ARM SLEIGH wraps around every VERSION_7M special-register move folds away. Twelve `ARMTHUMBinstructions.sinc` constructors (`mrs`/`msr` against ipsr, primask, basepri, basepri_max, faultmask and control) model the move as a RUNTIME privilege test -- `b:1 = isCurrentModePrivileged(); if (!b) goto <notPriv>; <the real effect>` -- so kuna, lowering the model literally, gives every MRS/MSR one extra basic block and two extra CFG edges that exist in no source. A four-instruction `irq_disable`/`irq_restore` pair therefore lands four phantom branches in the middle of an otherwise straight-line function. On, a synthesized `<callotherfixup>` makes the user-op return the constant 1: the condition constant-folds, the guard block and its edges die, and the real effect survives unchanged. Registered at architecture bootstrap on any language that declares the user-op (i.e. ARM) and gated at the CALLOTHER consumption seam, so off the emitted C is byte-identical to a build without the fixup. IDA and Binary Ninja both model MRS/MSR as a plain intrinsic with no test at all; upstream Ghidra shares kuna's defect.
- **When to flip:** On by default: Cortex-M firmware whose C would otherwise be broken into extra `if (isCurrentModePrivileged())` blocks around every interrupt-mask or special-register access, or whose CFG would carry branches the source has no `if` for, renders the straight-line access. The assumption is a MODELLING JUDGEMENT, not a proof: Cortex-M Thread mode really can run unprivileged (CONTROL.nPRIV = 1) and those moves really do read as zero there. Flip off when auditing code that is meant to run unprivileged, or to see the hardware model exactly as the SLEIGH spells it. Inert on every non-ARM target and on any ARM function with no MRS/MSR.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/inline-inject · ida · correctness-fix · kuna-cortexmpriv
- **Example:** `option cortexmpriv on`

### `tailcalljump` -- on | direct | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** leaf function ends in a (*dat_...)(...) computed call with a 'Treating indirect jump as call' warning; jmp to a plt stub inlined into the caller instead of a named tail call; plt thunk body absorbed where func(...) is expected; a veneer renders as switch(0x...) with one case holding another function's body, or halt_missing() with a 'flows out of bounds' warning.
- **What it does:** Recover an -O2 tail jump (a direct `jmp` to another function's entry, e.g. `jmp setlocale@plt`) as a tail call (CALL + RETURN) so the callee resolves by name and its return value flows out, instead of flowing into the callee (which inlines a PLT thunk and mis-renders it as a `(*dat_...)(...)` indirect call with a 'Treating indirect jump as call' warning). A caller-declared extent containing a direct or recovered computed branch target keeps that branch intraprocedural, even if discovery knows the target as a function entry. A terminal conditional branch to another known function entry outside an explicit extent becomes a call and return only on its taken path, under both `on` and `direct`; its false path keeps flowing normally. Unknown, mid-function and unbounded conditional targets keep the original flow and clipping policy. `on` also takes a computed jump whose recovered jump table names one destination, when that destination is another known function's entry: an ARM veneer or long-branch stub (`ldr r1,[pc]; bx r1`, `ldr pc,[pc,#-4]`), an x86 `jmp *GOT` in a `-fno-plt` build, or a jump through a read-only function-pointer slot, which kuna otherwise renders as a one-case `switch` copying the callee's body in, or as `halt_missing()` when the stub's exact extent is declared. That jump becomes the same tail call when the destination lies outside the function's declared extent, or when no explicit extent is supplied and the callee's prototype is stated (declared, DWARF, a library signature, a demangled C++ name), so it fixes the call's arguments, and either that prototype states a `void` return or the function's own output is stated, so the return value reaches it. A prototype with no return type (a demangled C++ name) leaves the return unknown, not `void`. Otherwise the copied-in body stays: it states the arguments and return value a call could not. The register that carried the target address is never taken as an argument of the call. `direct` recovers only direct jumps. When it fires it logs a `tailcalljump: recovered tail call` warning at the branch site so the introduced call is observable. Under `on`, a one-destination computed jump to a function with no bytes, or to one a callee-first decompile-all filed as losing nothing to a call, is a tail call as well (the GOT-slot rule of `kuna_gottailcall.rs`).
- **When to flip:** On by default. A leaf function ends in `jmp <func>@plt` and kuna would emit `(*dat_...)(...)` + a 'Treating indirect jump as call' marker instead of `func(...)`, or a veneer (an ARM long-branch stub, an x86 `-fno-plt` `jmp *GOT`) renders as `switch(0x...)` with one case, or as `halt_missing()` with a 'flows out of bounds' warning under a declared extent. Set `direct` to keep direct-jump tail calls but follow a veneer's computed jump into its destination as before; set `off` to restore the upstream flow-into-callee rendering for both (the two affected datatests, Long double #1/#2, opt out per-test).
- **Where / provenance:** P2/flow-classification · angr · structure-recovery · angr-tee-O2-tail-jumps
- **Example:** `option tailcalljump direct`

### `tailcallframe` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** a function decompiled by address continues into an unrelated function's body; an event/listener callback emits a second routine's UI strings and callees; the same callee is emitted twice in one function, once as a named call and once inlined; an unconditional jmp after add rsp,N; pop reg is followed instead of ending the function; kuna emits thousands of lines for a function the disassembly shows is a few hundred bytes.
- **What it does:** REMOVES CODE: recover a direct `jmp` as a tail call when the instructions ending at it tear down EXACTLY the frame the entry block built, even though the target is not a known function. `tailcalljump` asks `query_call(dest).is_some()`, so it only fires on a callee some discovery oracle already found; a callee reached only through a code pointer in initialized data satisfies none of them (the recursive-descent walk never enters the callback, so it never sees the callback's `call`), and the tail `jmp` is then followed as ordinary intraprocedural flow and the whole callee is decoded into the caller. This measures two constant stack-pointer deltas over the raw p-code -- forward from the function entry over the run that establishes the frame, backward from the branch over the run that ends at it -- and fires when the second is a strictly positive teardown of exactly the first. Both scans stop at the first control-flow op, at a stack-pointer write that is not `SP = SP +/- <const>` (a `leave`-style `SP = FP` restore declines), at a non-adjacent instruction address, and after 24 instructions. A frameless leaf can never match (no frame torn down = no evidence, and an intraprocedural jump would be indistinguishable). The rule also declines a target inside an explicit caller-declared extent, a target this function has already decoded, and the function's own entry. Logs a `tailcallframe: recovered tail call` WARNING at the branch site. The teardown must also give back what the entry block saved (the restore test of `kuna_tailcallsaved.rs`), so cdecl argument cleanup after a call -- `add esp,N` with the saved registers still on the stack -- is never read as a teardown.
- **When to flip:** A function decompiled by address runs on into an unrelated function's body -- the output starts with the code you asked for and continues through a second routine's logic, strings and callees -- and the disassembly shows an unconditional `jmp` to that routine right after a stack-frame teardown (`add rsp,N; pop reg; jmp X`). Typical of an indirect-only callback (an event/listener/vtable entry) in a stripped binary, where the callee is not in `kuna functions` and so `tailcalljump` cannot see it. On by default; flip OFF to restore the flow-into-the-callee decode.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/flow-classification · ida · correctness-fix · direct-address-keyboard-handler
- **Example:** `option tailcallframe off`

### `funcboundflow` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** a function's tail is really the body of the NEXT function; dead/garbage code after a call to a die()/fatal()/throw wrapper that never returns; two adjacent functions merged into one, the second also decompiled on its own; uninitialized reads in the tail after an unrecognized no-return call; halt_baddata() Bad instruction - Truncating control flow here right after a call on ARM32, where the words after the call are constants the function loads PC-relatively.
- **What it does:** REMOVES CODE: bound a function's fall-through at the entry of another known function. A kuna FunctionSymbol has no extent and CALL is fall-through, so a function whose last act is a `call` to a no-return routine kuna cannot prove no-return (in a stripped static binary: the unnamed `exit`/`abort`/`__stack_chk_fail` bodies and the app-level `die()`/`throw` wrappers built on them) runs its flow past the compiler's inter-function padding straight into the next function's entry and decodes THAT function's body into itself (the merge bug). When a fall-through reaches a known function entry (`query_call(next).is_some()`) not included in an explicit caller-declared extent, plant a no-return artificial RETURN and stop, emitting a `funcboundflow` truncation WARNING. Excludes the function's own entry and admits one safe shared-epilogue shape: if the complete instruction at the foreign entry is an unconditional CPUI_RETURN with no other control transfer, decode that instruction because it has no successor and therefore cannot consume the function after it. Branch, computed-branch, and conditional-return entries stay bounded, and a failed entry decode is conservative. On ARM32 the same bound holds at the function's own literal pool: when an unconditional CALL/CALLIND's fall-through lands on a pool the analysis tier proved (`listing/kuna_poolextents.rs`: maximal runs of 4-aligned executable words that a whole-word load reads at a fixed address from a trusted instruction that no fixed-address load reads as data and no known function entry separates from the word, with no trusted instruction covering or branching to the word, where trusted means reachable from a function entry without falling through a call, indirect call or user operation whose callee is not proven to return to the instruction after the call, or, in a second strict judgement whose words also count, without falling through any call at all), or up to one instruction of do-nothing alignment padding before one, in non-writable image bytes, the compiler put the pool there because the call does not return: the walk plants the no-return halt in the call's block and stops with a `funcboundflow` pool warning, instead of decoding the constants as instructions until one fails to decode (`halt_baddata()` / `Bad instruction`) or a decoded constant carries the walk into code the call never returns to. The pools are a fact of the Listing (`option listing`), so without it (`--mode fast`, and under `auto` at 2 MiB and above) and on every other target no call is bounded at a pool.
- **When to flip:** A function shows a garbage tail that is really the body of the FOLLOWING function (dead code after a call to a die()/throw/exit wrapper, uninitialized reads, a second unrelated function inlined after an error call). On by default; flip OFF to restore the upstream flow-into-the-next-function behavior.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/flow-classification · ida · correctness-fix · interp-bee-func-merge
- **Example:** `option funcboundflow off`

### `overlapbranch` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** a call to a sub_<hex> address that is not in the binary; writes through pointers that are never assigned right after a short conditional jump; a bogus dat_<hex> global incremented once and never read; a comparison whose operands are unreadable CONCAT/subpiece salad in hand-written or obfuscated code.
- **What it does:** REMOVES CODE: when a conditional branch's own target lies STRICTLY INSIDE the encoding of the instruction at its fall-through, the fall-through decode has swallowed the branch target -- the classic anti-disassembly junk-lead-byte overlap (`75 01 e8` : a `JNZ +1` over an `e8` byte that turns the real stream into a bogus 5-byte CALL). kuna's flow follower pops the fall-through before the branch target, so the bogus decode wins by arrival order and desynchronises everything downstream; `set_fallthru_bound` only notices afterwards, when the losing stream is already built. This option makes the explicitly encoded branch target win: the ops of the overlapping fall-through decode are dropped, an artificial halt is planted at its own address (the conditional and its fall-through EDGE both survive), and the target is decoded on its own boundary. Two real instruction starts cannot sit at `next` and strictly inside `next`, so whenever it fires at least one of the two decodes was already wrong. ONE legitimate overlap is excluded first, and it is compiler-generated: glibc's conditional-`LOCK` idiom (`74 01` hopping over an `f0` prefix byte, as in a statically linked `_int_free`/`_int_malloc`) is the SAME instruction with its prefix taken or skipped, so the two decodes END AT THE SAME ADDRESS and both streams are real. The branch target's own instruction length is therefore decoded and the rule declines whenever `target + target_len == curaddr + step`, and likewise whenever the target does not decode at all. Ablating that one exclusion deletes the atomic store on a live path, so it is not decoration.
- **When to flip:** A hand-written / obfuscated / anti-disassembly binary decompiles with a call to an address outside the image, stores through never-assigned pointers, or bogus `dat_<hex>` globals right after a short conditional jump. Off restores the upstream fall-through-wins decode. Inert on ordinary compiler output: the trigger needs a branch target strictly inside its own fall-through instruction, and the one compiler idiom that produces that (a conditional jump over a `LOCK` prefix) is excluded because both decodes end at the same address.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/flow-classification · ida · correctness-fix · overlapping-anti-disassembly-sequence
- **Example:** `option overlapbranch off`

### `cleanupcode` -- on | off, default `on` (destructive opt-in)

- **Symptoms:** core::ptr::drop_in_place(...) calls all over a decompiled rust function; drop glue and deallocation calls that are nowhere in the rust source; Drop::drop / __rust_dealloc / RawVecInner::deallocate noise at every scope exit; rust output is twice as long as the source because of automatic resource management; flip off to see when a rust value is actually dropped or freed.
- **What it does:** REMOVES CODE: delete the Rust drop/deallocate call sites. Rust emits a drop-glue call at every scope exit and every `?` early return, so decompiled Rust is dominated by `core::ptr::drop_in_place<...>(v)` lines that appear nowhere in the source and carry no meaning for a reader. A direct CALL whose recovered callee name normalizes to one of `core::ptr::drop_in_place`, `core::ops::drop::Drop::drop`, `alloc::raw_vec::RawVecInner::deallocate`, `__rust_dealloc` or `__rustc::__rust_dealloc` is destroyed in the PRE-SSA window (the top of mainloop, gated on heritage pass 0), which is the point of the timing: the register/stack writes that existed only to set up the drop's arguments lose their last reader and are collected by the ordinary ActionDeadCode fixpoint, so the argument setup goes with the call instead of being left behind as unexplained assignments. Normalization reproduces the Oxidizer matcher: un-escape the legacy rustc `$LT$`/`$GT$`/`$u20$` mangling, then collapse the innermost angle-bracket group repeatedly - deleting a plain generic argument list and replacing a `<T as Trait>` qualified path with the TRAIT name - so `_$LT$alloc..vec..Vec$LT$T$C$A$GT$$u20$as$u20$core..ops..drop..Drop$GT$::drop` matches and `FakeCrypt::fileops::drop_ransom_note` does not. Oxidizer's `free`/`close`/`_close` entries are deliberately NOT carried: kuna's primary corpus is C binaries and deleting `free()` would be a catastrophically wrong answer. The remaining names cannot occur in a C program, which is what makes the pass structurally inert on a C binary and lets it default ON with no compiler-detection channel from the loader.
- **When to flip:** On by default (DIV-81). A Rust binary whose functions are dominated by drop_in_place/dealloc glue that is not in the source. Flip OFF to keep every drop and deallocation call site - e.g. when auditing a use-after-free, reasoning about when a resource is actually released, or matching the binary instruction-for-instruction. Inert on any binary with no Rust drop symbols, so C/C++ output is byte-identical either way.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/flow-classification · oxidizer · presentation-default · oxidizer-CleanupCodeRemover
- **Example:** `option cleanupcode off`

### `linuxsyscall` -- off | auto | on, default `auto`

- **Symptoms:** a syscall renders as (*(void *)swi(0x80))() - a call through a pointer nothing assigns; the mov $N,%eax before an int 0x80 has vanished from the output; an int 0x80 site shows no arguments even though the disassembly loads ebx/ecx/edx; 32-bit linux _start or shellcode where every system call is an unnamed indirect call; esp-relative locals shift by four bytes after an int 0x80.
- **What it does:** On an x86 Linux ELF, render a 32-bit `int 0x80` as the syscall it is instead of an indirect call through the `swi` userop. x86 SLEIGH lowers `INT imm8` to `intloc = swi(imm8); call [intloc]` (ia.sinc:3671) - the honest lifting of a general software interrupt, since SLEIGH cannot know which operating system is behind the vector - and the decompiler renders that as `(*(void *)swi(0x80))();`: a call through a pointer nothing assigns, with the syscall number and every argument erased, because the register writes that set them up have no reader left and the dead-code fixpoint collects them. On 32-bit Linux the vector is fixed and so is the ABI: the number is in EAX and the arguments are EBX, ECX, EDX, ESI, EDI, EBP, with the result back in EAX. This pass recognizes the lowering structurally (a two-input CALLOTHER whose second input is the one-byte vector constant 0x80, feeding a CALLIND at the same instruction address), reads the number from a backward walk of the basic block that accepts only a full-width `EAX = <constant>`, and retargets the CALLIND in place onto a call spec named `sys_<name>` whose input prototype is LOCKED to the first N argument registers - so the later ActionFuncLink materializes the argument Varnodes itself and the `mov $1,%ebx` that feeds the call keeps a reader. The synthesized spec also sets extrapop = 0: `int 0x80` pushes no return address, where the default __cdecl extrapop of 4 (what the indirect call gets today) hands ESP back four bytes it never lost and shifts every later ESP-relative reference in the function. Three refusals leave the old rendering untouched rather than guess: a number that is not a locally-resolvable constant, a number with no vetted entry in the syscall table (332 of the 438 `__NR_` names - the arity has to be known, because printing a name with the wrong argument count is a false statement about the call, not a partial one), and any language that is not x86. `auto` (the default) adds a fourth: the loaded image must be an ELF whose EI_OSABI is System V or GNU/Linux and that carries no other system's ABI-tag note - never a BSD or Solaris OSABI, never a PE, Mach-O or raw image - because the vector alone does not prove the operating system behind it; `on` drops that test for shellcode and raw images.
- **When to flip:** On (`auto`) by default: a 32-bit Linux ELF - typically hand-written assembly, a static `_start` or a packer stub - whose output would otherwise contain `(*(void *)swi(0x80))();` with the syscall arguments vanished renders `sys_write(1,&buf,n)`, with the prototype locked to the registers the table says the call reads. Inert on every non-x86 language, on any image that is not a Linux ELF (a BSD or Solaris OSABI, a PE, a Mach-O, raw bytes), and on any int 0x80 site whose number it cannot resolve. Set `on` for shellcode or a raw image whose OS the container cannot state; `off` keeps the `swi` rendering.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/flow-classification · kuna · correctness-fix · kuna-linux-int80-syscall
- **Example:** `option linuxsyscall on`

### `msvcstrappend` -- on | off, default `off` (destructive opt-in)

- **Symptoms:** several near-identical if/else blocks in a row, each comparing two adjacent stack slots and either calling a helper with the same object or storing one character through a 16-byte-threshold pointer select; an msvc c++ function whose string-building code shows a `0x10 <= v` buffer select before every character store; a loop body that is a whole capacity check plus a grow call to append one byte to a std::string; counting inlined std::string appends from the c output gives the wrong number.
- **What it does:** REMOVES CODE: collapses each inlined MSVC x64 `std::string` character append into one call. MSVC inlines `push_back` (which `operator+=(char)` is) and the literal form of `append(const char *, size_t)` at every call site as a capacity diamond over the string object: load `_Mysize` (+16) and `_Myres` (+24), and on the fast arm store `_Mysize + n`, pick the buffer with `_Myres > 15 ? _Bx._Ptr : _Bx._Buf`, and write the bytes plus a terminating zero at `ptr[_Mysize]`; on the slow arm call `_Reallocate_grow_by`. Every such append prints as the same five-to-ten-line `if`/`else` block, so a run of appends is a run of near-identical blocks whose count carries the meaning. The pass proves the diamond on the raw p-code before heritage, by symbolic execution of the head, every fast-arm path and the grow block: the head branches to the fast arm exactly when `_Mysize < _Myres` (or `_Myres - _Mysize >= n`), decided exactly over a test set complete for the comparisons it admits; each fast path stores `_Mysize + n` to the size slot and exactly `n` bytes and a zero at `ptr[_Mysize]` and nothing else, with `ptr` the object on every path taken only when `_Myres <= 15` and the loaded pointer on every path taken only when `_Myres > 15`, both kinds present; the grow block is one direct call receiving the object in `RCX` and the same character in `R9B` (or the count in `RDX` and, in `R9`, a pointer into read-only memory whose image bytes are the stored bytes); no register either arm writes is one the default model preserves; and no op after the join reads a register byte the rewrite changes before overwriting it, up to the next call or return. It then removes the fast-arm edge, replaces the grow block's argument setup, and gives its call a locked `void std::string::push_back(void *this, char c)` or `std::string::append(void *this, char *s, size_t n)` prototype that returns `this` only when every fast path left the object in `RAX`; a register the model kills at a call but no fast path writes is declared preserved by it, so later calls keep the argument evidence the fast path carried. The grow callee's body is never read: a call handed exactly the append's arguments on the capacity-exhausted edge is taken to be the reallocating append. Any unproven element leaves the diamond untouched: a small-string threshold other than 15, a grow call handed a different character, an extra store, a count the grow arm takes from a register set outside the head, a scratch register or flag read after the join. x86-64 under a Win64-shaped model (`RSI`/`RDI` preserved) only; inert on every other language and ABI.
- **When to flip:** Flip ON when reading an MSVC x64 C++ binary whose functions build strings character by character: each `s += c` / `s.push_back(c)` otherwise prints as its own capacity check, `// branch-flip` marker and grow call, and a password or format string assembled from several appends reads as a stack of identical blocks. Default OFF because it is destructive -- it deletes the inlined fast path's stores and renames the grow call to a library name the binary does not contain, trusting the grow call's argument shape rather than its body -- and because no MSVC C++ corpus in the tree can measure it. Off also restores the raw rendering when auditing the inlined code itself.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/flow-classification · kuna · opt-in-tool · GH-468
- **Example:** `option msvcstrappend on`

### `switchselector` -- on | off, default `off`

- **Symptoms:** a re-rolled switch dispatches on a function parameter and the compiler's if/else-if chain would read better; a callback or window/dialog procedure's message dispatch reads better as the chain the compiler emitted; option loweredswitch off gives the rendering you want, but you want it for one cascade and not for the whole binary.
- **What it does:** Record a lowered-switch cascade only when the switch value is computed inside the function; a cascade that dispatches on a parameter is left exactly as the compiler lowered it. `loweredswitch` re-rolls a compiler-lowered comparison cascade into a `switch`, and both renderings read the same value, so which one is better is a judgement call, not a correctness question. On a callback shape - a Win32 window or dialog procedure dispatching on its message parameter - the chain is often the more faithful rendering: it names the parameter at every arm and keeps the compiler's own ordering, where the re-rolled `switch` presents the dispatch as if the function had derived the selector itself. With this on, only a cascade whose switch variable has a defining op here - a call return, a load, a computed value - is re-rolled. Detection runs on the fully simplified, SSA'd graph, so `computed here` is exactly `the Varnode is written`. `loweredswitch off` remains the whole-pass escape hatch.
- **When to flip:** You want the compiler's own if/else-if chain back for a cascade that dispatches on a parameter, without turning `loweredswitch` off for the whole binary - typically a callback, window procedure or dialog procedure whose message parameter is the switch value. A declined cascade renders exactly as `option loweredswitch off` renders it, and every cascade over a value the function computes (a getopt return, a table load) still re-rolls. MEASURED: byte-identical on the 675-assertion datatest corpus with the guard forced on.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/switch-model · kuna · structure-recovery · kuna-loweredswitch-parameter-selector
- **Example:** `option switchselector on`

### `int3pad` -- off | warn | halt, default `warn`

- **Symptoms:** an int3 pad renders as (*(void *)swi(3))() - a call through a pointer nothing assigns; a function returns the result of a call through swi(3); nothing in the C says control ran into a run of 0xcc padding bytes; an anti-debug binary's clean-run path ends in an indirect call that only the disassembly explains.
- **What it does:** Name the `int3` pad control ran into, instead of printing it as a call through a pseudo-op. x86 SLEIGH lowers `INT3` to `intloc = swi(3); call [intloc]; return [0:1]` (ia.sinc:3670) - honest lifting, since SLEIGH cannot know what sits behind the vector - and the printer renders that as `v1 = (void *)swi(3); return (*v1)();`, which reads as an ordinary call through a function pointer. Nothing in the C says the byte at that address is `0xcc`, that it is one of a run of them, or that control got there by running off the end of the decoded code; the pad is visible only in `kuna disassemble`. `warn` (the default) recognizes the lowering structurally - a CALLIND reading the storage a `swi` CALLOTHER with the 1-byte constant vector 3 wrote in the same instruction - counts the `0xcc` bytes at the site, and buffers a warning the P9 slug table renders as `// int3-pad xN`. `halt` additionally marks the call spec no-return and plants the artificial halt, so the pad ends the flow instead of contributing the fabricated return value of `return (*v1)();`.
- **When to flip:** On (`warn`) by default: it adds a comment and changes nothing else, so a decoded `int3` is named wherever one is reached. Set `halt` when reading anti-debug code whose clean-run path falls into a pad and the fabricated `return (*(void *)swi(3))();` is in the way - it is not the default because a debugger attached to the process can step past an `int3`, so ending the flow is a judgement about the pad rather than a fact about the encoding. Set `off` to restore the unannotated upstream rendering. Shape-gated on the `swi` vector 3, so `int 0x29` (Windows __fastfail, see `fastfailnoreturn`), `int 0x80` (Linux, see `linuxsyscall`) and every non-x86 language are untouched; structurally inert wherever no `int3` is decoded, and byte-identical (0/675) on the datatest corpus. The pad length is a loader read: when it fails, or when the encoding is the two-byte `INT 0x03` rather than `0xcc`, the warning is emitted without a count rather than with a guessed one.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/flow-classification · kuna · presentation-default · GH-468
- **Example:** `option int3pad halt`

### `x64syscall` -- off | on | abi, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** an x86-64 syscall renders as syscall() with empty parens, with the number and every argument erased; a syscall wrapper returns its own first parameter, the syscall number, instead of the syscall's result; the register writes feeding a SYSCALL are all missing from the C while kuna disassemble shows them; a SYSCALL's result is never assigned to anything.
- **What it does:** On x86-64, give the `SYSCALL` user-op the Linux kernel ABI's register effects, so a syscall wrapper stops returning its own first argument. `ia.sinc:4836` lowers the instruction as `RCX = inst_next; R11 = rflags; syscall();` - a CALLOTHER with NO inputs and NO output - and that one fact produces both halves of the damage. No inputs: the register writes that set the call up have no reader, the dead-code fixpoint collects them, and the number and every argument are erased, so the op prints as `syscall()` with empty parens. No output: nothing redefines RAX across the instruction, so the RAX a wrapper stores afterwards is still the one it loaded from its own `number` parameter and the function is emitted as `syscall(); return number;` - correct copy propagation over an operation kuna has been told writes nothing, which makes the emitted C a false statement about the program. On, the CALLOTHER is rewritten in place before heritage to read RAX and the argument registers and to write RAX; the reads keep the setup alive and the write retires the false return. `linuxsyscall` does not cover this and cannot be extended to it: there is no CALLIND here to retarget (a bare CALLOTHER, not the `int 0x80` `intloc = swi(0x80); call [intloc]` pair), the number is a runtime parameter rather than a constant it could look up, and it is gated to x86-32. On the exact GCC AMD64 target with its ordinary SysV function and evaluation models and real RSP stack, recognized rewritten calls also have unknown effects on writable data and stack memory: stores observed by the kernel stay before the instruction, post-call loads reload the buffer, and values saved before one or two calls remain separate. Windows targets and MSABI models retain the existing register-only effects and ordering. RCX and R11 are already written by the SLEIGH constructor and are left alone; a CALLOTHER a compiler spec has specialized with its own `<callotherfixup>` is declined, so a spec-declared model always wins.
- **When to flip:** On by default (`on`): any x86-64 function containing a `SYSCALL` - hand-written asm wrappers, static binaries, shellcode, a libc `syscall()` - reads its number and arguments and writes its result, instead of printing `syscall();` with empty parens or returning the incoming syscall number. With a RUNTIME number nothing can say how many of the six argument registers the callee reads, so the read set is a modelling judgement, and the two values are that judgement: `on` takes an argument register only where a bounded backward walk of the CALLOTHER's own basic block finds it written before the instruction, so every read is of a value the function demonstrably places there and no undefined register is ever introduced - the cost is that a wrapper whose setup sits in a predecessor block keeps the old rendering for that argument. Set `abi` for such a wrapper: it takes all six unconditionally, which is what the kernel contract permits the callee to read, at the price that a register the function never writes reads as an undefined input and can add a parameter the source has not got. Inert on every language but x86-64 (RAX and all six argument registers must resolve at 8 bytes and the default code space must be 8 bytes wide) and on any function with no SYSCALL. Flip off to keep the zero-effect CALLOTHER.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/flow-classification · kuna · correctness-fix · kuna-x64syscall
- **Example:** `option x64syscall abi`

### `syscallregs` -- off | auto | on, default `auto`

- **Symptoms:** a function containing svc/ecall/syscall/sc returns its arguments as a register pair (CONCAT44 or undefined16); a MIPS syscall wrapper returns the syscall number it loaded into v0; software_interrupt(0), CallSupervisor(0), ecall() or syscall() shows no arguments while the disassembly loads registers before it; a test of a system call's result tests the argument the function set up instead; a syscall wrapper returns its own first parameter; the same wrapper is right in a linked Linux program but wrong in its .o or a static musl build; a MIPS syscall wrapper grows a fourth parameter a3 it tests after the syscall; a PowerPC syscall wrapper tests an uninitialized cr0 after sc; a MIPS syscall wrapper that passes its parameters straight to the kernel shows none of them.
- **What it does:** Give the system-call instruction of ARM and AArch64 (`svc`), RISC-V (`ecall`), MIPS (`syscall`) and PowerPC (`sc`) the registers it reads and writes, so the value a function reads back after the call is the call's result. The SLEIGH specs lower each of them to a CALLOTHER with no register inputs and no output, so kuna is told nothing changes: whatever the function put in the result register (`r0`, `x0`, `a0`, `v0`, `r3`) to set the call up is still there afterwards. A wrapper that moves its arguments into place returns them as a register pair (`return CONCAT44(a0,a1);`), a MIPS wrapper returns the syscall number it loaded into `v0` (`return 0xfa4;`), and a later test of the result tests the argument instead. When it acts, the CALLOTHER is rewritten in place before heritage: it writes the result register, and it reads the number register and then the argument registers in order, each only while the function writes it on every path to the call with no call in between, so a printed argument is always in its own position and no undefined register becomes a parameter. The pair goes away with it: return recovery treats the rewritten call as a call site, so a value it reads as an argument is not also a returned half, even where the function discards the result and the kernel-preserved argument register still reaches the RETURN, and the same value stays free to be the next call's argument. On MIPS and PowerPC the call also writes the register the kernel flags a failure in, `a3` (0 or 1) or `cr0` (its summary-overflow bit), with an opaque `syscall_error()` placed right after it, so the C library's test after the call reads that flag rather than the function's entry `a3` (a phantom fourth parameter) or a `cr0` nothing set; each flag is its own value (two calls' flags are never folded or merged into one), it is never taken as a later call's argument, and it is printed at its definition when another call or system call comes between it and its use. That phantom `a3` used to pull a MIPS wrapper's real parameters in with it, so a MIPS system call also reads, written or not, up to as many argument registers as the kernel's entry point for its constant number takes (a table built from the kernel's o32/n32/n64 syscall tables), and up to all of `a0`..`a3` when the number is not a known constant, each only while no call can have changed it since the function's entry or its write (o32 does not preserve `a0`..`a3` across a call): a `read` wrapper that hands its three parameters to the kernel in place keeps them, and no value from before a call is printed as an argument. `auto` acts only on an image the loader identified as a program for an operating system's user space (an ELF with a Linux/BSD `EI_OSABI`, a `PT_INTERP`, a dynamic section naming a shared object, or an ABI-tag note), because a bare-metal RTOS uses the same instruction for a context switch or a privilege change and keeps live values in the result register across it; `on` acts on any image. Writable default-data and stack ranges have unknown effects across the call, so a buffer loaded after the instruction reads memory the kernel may have replaced instead of the pre-call stored value. A CALLOTHER a compiler spec has specialized with its own `<callotherfixup>` is left alone, and x86-64 keeps its own model (`x64syscall`).
- **When to flip:** Default `auto`: on a Linux or BSD program or shared library the kernel returns a value in the result register, so the system call writes it there. Set `on` for an image that does not say what system it runs on but whose system calls do return a value: a relocatable object, a raw image, a statically linked musl or uClibc program (no ABI note), or an RTOS that returns in the result register. Do not set `on` for bare-metal code whose SVC handler preserves the registers (FreeRTOS's `svc 2` privilege raise and `svc 0`/`ecall`/`sc` yields): the call then hides the value the function kept in the result register. Set `off` to restore the vendored zero-effect CALLOTHER everywhere. Limits: outside MIPS, arguments a wrapper hands to the kernel untouched are not read, and the argument list stops at the first of them, so a pass-through wrapper prints the number alone and a later argument the function does write is left out too (and can then still be taken as the high half of a returned pair, as with `off`); on MIPS a call whose number is not a known constant (a `syscall` dispatcher) reads `a0`..`a3`, so a test of its flag still reads as a fourth parameter there; a call that sets up fewer registers than the kernel's entry takes, with no call before it, shows the rest as the function's parameters (the kernel does read them); a register that crossed a call is not read, which stops the list there as without the table; and the o32 arguments past `a3` the kernel takes from the stack are not read; the MIPS `v1` a few calls return a second value in is not modelled; an image whose handler preserves `a3` or `cr0` reads the opaque flag where it kept its own value; a function that really returns, as the high half of a 64-bit value, a register it also handed to the kernel loses that half. MEASURED: byte-identical (0/675) on the datatest corpus, where `auto` is inert by construction (the XML bootstrap sets no loader fact). decompile-all `auto` vs `off` over 25 stripped binaries (24,212 functions): the 12 with no operating-system marker are byte-identical -- 7 ARM firmware images (U-Boot, NuttX, FreeRTOS, ChibiOS, Betaflight, Cleanflight, Crazyflie), FreeRTOS RTOSDemo, p2im, a static uClibc MIPS busybox, two RISC-V Keystone enclaves -- and so are two x86-64 Linux programs, where the option does not apply, and the PowerPC64 loader, which has no system call. In the other 10 Linux images (the glibc loaders of AArch64, ARM EABI, ARM hard-float, MIPS, PowerPC and PowerPC64LE, AArch64 libc.so.6, an ARM hard-float server, a MIPS program and a static PowerPC64LE program) 954 functions containing a system call change: 157 register-pair returns become single returns; 5 wrappers that pass their first argument through and write a later one (`sigpending`, `pipe`, `symlink`) now return a pair whose low half is the result, where `off` returned the later argument register on the success path. Another 528 functions without one change, 374 only in variable numbering and the rest in types, casts or arguments inherited from the wrappers they call. The MIPS/PowerPC error flag (GH-857), decompile-all before vs after over 26 images (34,482 functions): 3,426 functions change, all in 19 Linux MIPS and PowerPC images (C libraries, loaders, libgomp and static programs); two static uClibc busyboxes, an AArch64 loader, a PowerPC64 loader and three small MIPS programs are byte-identical. 2,715 now test `syscall_error()` where they read the entry `a3` or an unset `cr0`, among them wrappers whose error test had folded to a constant because they loaded `a3` as the fourth argument (`lutimes` always returned -1, `getcontext` always took its error path); 149 show a system call's arguments it did not read before or a caller dropping the phantom argument its callee lost; 551 are struct renumbering and 11 type spellings inherited from a changed callee. No MIPS function loses a parameter its C prototype has: of the 785 that print fewer parameters than before, the 555 that glibc's headers declare by name keep every register parameter they declare (the variadic `open`/`open64`, `ioctl`, `fcntl` and `sysmips` lose only the phantom `a3`; the three with two parameters are the GLIBC_2.3.3 versions of `sched_getaffinity`, `sched_setaffinity` and `pthread_getaffinity_np`), and the other 230 drop only positions past the system call's kernel count, registers the function sets itself before the call, or (two setxid signal handlers) positions their code never reads; 57 gain parameters the kernel reads (`fchownat`'s flags, the `__mips_syscall5`/`6` dispatchers). 11 MIPS system calls print one argument fewer than before: the `a3` past the kernel's count that held an earlier call's error flag. A detector run over 11 MIPS images finds none of 2,222 forced register reads crossing a call.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/flow-classification · kuna · correctness-fix · kuna-syscallregs
- **Example:** `option syscallregs on`

### `switchmodbound` -- on | off, default `off` (destructive opt-in)

- **Symptoms:** switch reports 'Could not recover jumptable ... Too many branches' and renders as a computed call; indirect jump bounded only by a modulo or and-mask on its index never becomes a switch.
- **What it does:** Bound a LOAD-table jumptable by a modulo (index % N) or and-mask on its index when no guard bounds it.
- **When to flip:** Set on PER PROGRAM when a switch reports 'Could not recover jumptable ... Too many branches' and renders as a computed call; DESTRUCTIVE as a global default (may over-bound an unrelated indirect jump).
- **Where / provenance:** P2/switch-model · ghidra-upstream · opt-in-tool · GH-9191
- **Example:** `option switchmodbound on`

### `constselectjump` -- on | off, default `off` (destructive opt-in)

- **Symptoms:** indirect jump renders as a computed (code *)() call whose destinations are already constants in the emitted C; 'Treating indirect jump as call' on a CMOV/predicated dispatch; the body behind a conditional indirect branch is never decoded.
- **What it does:** Recover an indirect branch whose destination is selected between constant addresses (a CMOV/predicated dispatch) as a jump table over that constant set, instead of truncating it to a call.
- **When to flip:** An indirect jump renders as a computed `(*v)()` call carrying a 'Treating indirect jump as call' warning while the destinations are already visible as address constants in the emitted C, and the code behind them is missing. DESTRUCTIVE as a global default: a conditional TAIL CALL selecting between two nearby function entries is the same shape, and recovering it splices both callee bodies into the caller.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/switch-model · kuna · structure-recovery · re-conditional-indirect-branches-hide
- **Example:** `option constselectjump on`

### `switchguardbound` -- on | off, default `off` (destructive opt-in)

- **Symptoms:** 'Too many branches' jumptable failure where a cbranch range guard bounds the index; computed (code *)() call at a gcc sub/ja guarded dispatch with the index spilled to the stack.
- **What it does:** Bound a LOAD-table jumptable by an out-of-band CBRANCH range guard (idx LEu N) when the basic model's guard analysis could not (e.g. a GCC `sub LOW; ja DEFAULT` dispatch with the index spilled to the stack and the flag idiom not yet simplified).
- **When to flip:** Set on PER PROGRAM when a switch reports 'Could not recover jumptable ... Too many branches' and renders as a computed (code *)() call AND the dispatch is range-guarded (vs the modulo form switchmodbound handles); DESTRUCTIVE as a global default (the guard-to-index correspondence is asserted across a stack spill it cannot prove in dataflow, so it may over-bound an unrelated indirect jump).
- **Where / provenance:** P2/switch-model · angr · opt-in-tool · angr-missing-function-call
- **Example:** `option switchguardbound on`

### `highsliceguard` -- on | off, default `off`

- **Symptoms:** narrow comparison after a logical right shift does not bound a jump table; a high-byte table index renders as jump-as-call; a Rust match over a shifted tag is missing despite an unsigned bound.
- **What it does:** Match a logical right shift to the complete high-byte slice of the same SSA input, so a narrow comparison can bound the full-width jump-table index. Both offsets must be constant and byte-aligned, the slice must reach the input's high end, and the shift must retain the input's width. Arithmetic shifts, interior slices and unrelated inputs are rejected; existing signed, unsigned and wrapping range intersections retain their value sets.
- **When to flip:** Off in every preset. Enable when a narrow comparison after a logical right shift bounds a table but it renders as a computed call or reports too many branches. The exact guard identity recovers the missing switch without a non-zero-mask assumption. Measured enabled recovery added 10.8% median CPU and 11.2% median wall time on the pinned upstream walk_dir case, exceeding the 5% default speed budget; the original 675 datatest assertions were unchanged.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/switch-model · angr · structure-recovery · angr-amd64-single-block-jumptable
- **Example:** `option highsliceguard on`

### `switchsharedcase` -- on | off, default `on` (destructive opt-in)

- **Symptoms:** getopt-style switch inside a loop degrades to a computed call with goto spaghetti; pic relative-offset jump table with a loop-carried base register never recovered; 'Too many branches' on a dispatch whose table base is set before the loop.
- **What it does:** Recover a GCC PIC relative-offset jump table (target = base + sext(load4(base + idx*4))) whose table-base register is a loop-carried MULTIEQUAL: the `lea .rodata` base is set before a getopt-style loop while the BRANCHIND is inside it, so the path-meld collapses to the final base+offset add and the CBRANCH range guard on the load index never bounds the table. Rebuilds the meld as a clean single path down to the guarded index so the table resolves and the switch structures. On by default (DIV-14): SLOWER on the functions whose loop-carried switch it recovers (the extra meld-rebuild + table resolution walk runs there), but kept on for the better recovery quality; byte-identical (0/675) on every datatest, which has no such loop-carried PIC switch.
- **When to flip:** On by default (DIV-14): recovers a getopt/dispatch switch inside a loop that would otherwise report 'Could not recover jumptable ... Too many branches' and render as a computed (code *)() call with goto spaghetti. Flip OFF only if the heuristic mis-sizes or accepts an unrelated indirect jump on a specific program (it reads a read-only table at a base it recovers across a loop phi) — it is marked destructive for that reason, but it is byte-identical over the 675 datatests and kept on for quality despite being slower on the functions it recovers.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/switch-model · angr · opt-in-tool · angr-switch-case-shared-case-node
- **Example:** `option switchsharedcase on`

### `switchmultipred` -- on | off, default `on` (destructive opt-in)

- **Symptoms:** image-base-relative switch whose bound guard is duplicated across multiple predecessors renders as a computed call; 'Too many branches' where the dispatch block has several guarded incoming paths; msvc memmove small-count tail dispatch truncated to an indirect call.
- **What it does:** Recover an image-base-relative jump table (target = imagebase + load4(table + idx*4)) whose bound guard is 'unrolled' / duplicated across MULTIPLE predecessors of the dispatch block: the BRANCHIND's parent has sizeIn() > 1, each incoming path ending in its OWN (often semantically different) bound CBRANCH, the per-path switch indices meeting in a MULTIEQUAL. The single-predecessor guard walk short-circuits to checkUnrolledGuard, so no dominating guard bounds the table and the dispatch is truncated to a computed (code *)() call. When on, finds the dispatch MULTIEQUAL, evaluates each predecessor guard as a function of its MULTIEQUAL input, and re-bounds the table to [0, max-over-paths) so the readonly-LOAD table model recovers the switch (angr's 'abnormal switch case'). Also bounds the merged index when the copies of one bound check branch with opposite senses (one 'ja default', the other 'jbe dispatch'): each edge's check is pulled back to its own MULTIEQUAL input and the union of the per-edge ranges guards the MULTIEQUAL output, so a byte index no longer reads past the table into the next one.
- **When to flip:** Set on PER PROGRAM when an image-base-relative switch (e.g. an MSVC memmove/memcpy small-count tail dispatch) reports 'Could not recover jumptable ... Too many branches' and renders as a computed (code *)() call AND the dispatch block has multiple predecessors each with its own bound guard (vs the single-guard form switchguardbound handles); DESTRUCTIVE as a global default (it unions per-path guard prefixes across a MULTIEQUAL and re-binds the table from a heuristic max bound, so it may over-bind an unrelated multi-entry indirect jump).
- **Where / provenance:** P2/switch-model · angr · opt-in-tool · angr-abnormal-switch-case-case3
- **Example:** `option switchmultipred on`

### `unrolledguard` -- on | off, default `off` (destructive opt-in)

- **Symptoms:** one switch recovered but sibling interleaved jump tables degrade to computed calls; 'Could not find op at target address' during recovery of an msvc optimized memcpy dispatch; duff's-device tail dispatch rendered as 'Treating indirect jump as call'.
- **What it does:** Recover the interleaved jump tables of an MSVC optimized memcpy/memmove (Duff's device) at the partial-flow stage. The function holds several image-base-relative jump tables whose case bodies are reachable only as one another's case targets; kuna recovers them one at a time, each in its OWN fresh partial-flow clone. A later table's clone re-clones an already-recovered sibling table into its jumpvec, and that partial's collectEdges then calls target() on a sibling case body that was never decoded into THIS partial's visited snapshot (it is only decoded into the parent flow after the recovery pass returns), throwing 'Could not find op at target address' so the dispatch is truncated to a computed (code *)() call. Upstream avoids this by building one shared partial and running collectEdges once while the sibling tables are still empty. When on, the partial-clone collectEdges SKIPS an unresolvable recovered-table case-target edge (the same 'assume no branches out' shape the findJumpTable==0 partial path already uses) instead of throwing, so the interleaved tables all recover and the dispatches render as switches (angr's optimized memcpy).
- **When to flip:** Set on PER PROGRAM when a function holding several interleaved jump tables (e.g. an MSVC optimized memcpy/memmove Duff's-device tail dispatch) recovers ONE switch but degrades the OTHERS to 'Treating indirect jump as call' computed (code *)() calls, and the failures are flow-stage 'Could not find op at target address' on a sibling table's case body (NOT a guard-bound failure switchguardbound/switchmultipred would handle); DESTRUCTIVE as a global default (it suppresses an unresolved-case-target edge during partial-flow recovery, so on an unrelated truly-malformed table it could mask a real missing target instead of declining the table).
- **Where / provenance:** P2/switch-model · angr · opt-in-tool · angr-optimized-memcpy-6301a9
- **Example:** `option unrolledguard on`

### `jtsharepartial` -- on | off, default `on` (destructive opt-in)

- **Symptoms:** decompiling one function with several switch statements takes far longer than its size suggests; per-function latency scales with the NUMBER of jump tables rather than their size; profile shows the reduced jumptable action set running once per switch.
- **What it does:** Run the jump-table partial sub-decompilation ONCE per `recoverJumpTables` batch and share it across every table in that batch, the shape the C++ has (`Funcdata::stageJumpTable` guards the clone and the reduced pipeline behind `if (!partial.isJumptableRecoveryOn())`). Recovering a BRANCHIND means cloning the function's raw p-code into a partial Funcdata, building its blocks and running the reduced `jumptable` action set over it, so that the switch's index calculation simplifies to something the emulator can walk; kuna did that once PER TABLE, paying a whole sub-decompilation for every switch in the function. Sharing pays it once. Off restores the per-table re-clone, which is what `option unrolledguard` needs: its recovery of MSVC interleaved (Duff's-device) tables works precisely because a later table's fresh clone re-clones the siblings recovered before it, and a shared partial is built before any sibling has recovered.
- **When to flip:** Leave on. Flip OFF together with `option unrolledguard` on a function holding several INTERLEAVED jump tables whose case bodies are reachable only as one another's case targets (an MSVC optimized memcpy/memmove tail dispatch), where the per-table re-clone is what recovers the siblings; DESTRUCTIVE as a default in exactly that shape, since a shared partial cannot see an already-recovered sibling table. On a function with one jump table the two settings are structurally identical, and on an ordinary multi-table function sharing removes one full sub-decompilation per extra table.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/switch-model · ghidra · speed · decompiling-3396-byte-main
- **Example:** `option jtsharepartial off`

### `deadcascade` -- off | on | <n>, default `32`

- **Symptoms:** a huge function spends most of its time in oppool1; rule pool sweep count in the thousands for one function; each pool sweep removes only a handful of dead INDIRECT or MULTIEQUAL ops.
- **What it does:** Once one run of a rule pool has made N passes (default 32), when dead-op removal (`RuleEarlyRemoval`) takes out a join (MULTIEQUAL) or a guard (INDIRECT), also take out at once the joins and guards behind the pool's cursor that defined what it read and that nothing reads any more, and theirs in turn. The cursor has usually passed the op defining what a removed op read, so without this a chain of call guards and joins nothing reads dies one link per pool pass, and each pass sweeps the whole function (or, with `deadwaves`, walks it). The chain goes in the order the later passes would have removed it: one batch per pass, each in sequence order. Definitions at or ahead of the cursor, and dead ops of other kinds, are left to the passes as before. A run that has gone N passes is almost always taking such chains apart; a shorter run, which is nearly every run, removes as upstream does. Removing earlier than upstream changes when the other rules see a value lose a reader, which can change how variables merge, so the cascade waits for the long runs. `on` cascades from the first pass, `off` never.
- **When to flip:** Leave at the default. Set `off` to get upstream's one-link-per-pass removal everywhere, `on` or a smaller N to speed up functions whose pools run tens of passes, at the price of variable assignment that can differ from upstream's.
- **Where / provenance:** P3/simplification-quiescence · kuna · speed · GH-1034
- **Example:** `option deadcascade off`

### `nulterminator` -- on | off, default `off`

- **Symptoms:** a stack char buffer is declared one element short, e.g. [63] where the source has [64]; the NUL terminator after strncpy renders as an assignment to a separate char local; a stack char local is assigned 0 and never read, right after the end of an array; the buffer's last element is missing from the array and declared as its own variable.
- **What it does:** Keep the zero element that terminates an open stack character array inside the array, and close the array right after it (opt-in). ScopeLocal::restructure (varmap.cc:1294) extends an open RangeHint over a following hint only through RangeHint::attemptJoin (varmap.cc:170): within its highind, or a constant COPY no further than highind (isConstAbsorbable, varmap.cc:30); otherwise the open range ends where the next hint starts, so `strncpy(buf, s, sizeof(buf) - 1); buf[sizeof(buf) - 1] = 0;` prints `char buf[63]` beside a separate never-read char. With the option on, when attemptJoin declines the hint an open, unlocked char/UTF-16 range would end at and that hint is a plain constant-COPY slot of one element at a whole-element offset holding only unread zeros, the range becomes a fixed range ending one element after the slot (provided adjustFit keeps the extent and no plain frame address starts inside the array). DEFAULT OFF: the same frame shape -- an open char array followed by a lone unread zero at the next whole-element offset -- is produced by the struct-first-member idiom `struct { char name[32]; bool active; ... } u; strncpy(u.name, s, 32); u.active = 0; ...; f(&u);`, where the zero is a sibling FIELD read only through the base pointer, not the array's terminator. A spilled scalar whose value is read from a register looks identical too, so there is no frame-level way to tell a genuine terminator from a following field, and on by default this over-extends a correctly-sized array by one element. Flip on when reverse-engineering a string-heavy target where the buffers are known to be NUL-terminated strings, not struct members.
- **When to flip:** Off by default. Flip ON on a string-heavy target (an MSVC /GS function, a bounded strncpy/snprintf/read followed by an explicit NUL) to fold the terminator into the array: `char v3 [63]; char v8; // stack - 0x19` with `strncpy(v3,a0,0x3f); v8 = 0;` becomes `char v3 [64];` with `v3[0x3f] = 0;`. Keep it OFF on code with structs or records: the identical frame shape is also `struct { char name[N]; T field; }` initialized field by field then passed by pointer, and turning it on absorbs `field` into `name` (`char name[32]` -> `[33]`), inventing an element. gcc/clang and MSVC, every optimisation level. Inert unless a zero is stored at an open char array's next whole-element offset and never read directly.
- **Where / provenance:** P6/stack-frame-layout · kuna · opt-in-tool · GH-468
- **Example:** `option nulterminator on`

### `endptrbound` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** a pointer loop over a stack buffer ends at the address of an unrelated local (`while (v3 != v2)`); a loop's `while (p != vN)` names a local declared at the stack offset just past the buffer the loop reads; a stack buffer walked bytewise is declared as a scalar of the neighbour's width (`unsigned int v1;` for eight bytes); the walking pointer is typed after the neighbouring local instead of the bytes it reads.
- **What it does:** Recover a stack buffer that a proven pointer loop walks as one array spanning the walk, and express the loop's one-past-the-end bound on that buffer (`&buf[8]`) instead of as the address of whichever local happens to follow it.
- **When to flip:** On by default. With it OFF, `for (p = buf; p != buf + 8; p++)` over a stack buffer renders its bound as the next local (`while (v3 != v2)`), so the trip count is not readable from the C, and the neighbour's pointer type leaks into the walking pointer and into the buffer's declaration (`unsigned int v1;` for eight bytes). A walk counts only when it is proven: the pointer is the header phi of a natural loop that starts at a stack address and steps by one positive constant on every back edge; a comparison of it against a stack address a whole number of steps later (==, !=, p < end or end <= p) drives the branch that leaves the loop, from a block every back edge passes through; and every dereference through the pointer fits inside one step, with no call, store, other phi or variable offset able to read past it. The frame is left as it was when a hint straddles the range or is type-locked, a non-constant value inside it is typed or not exactly one element wide, typed index evidence inside it uses another element width (a byte walk over an `int` array), or a second walk crosses it; the array never extends further than the frame would otherwise have extended it. Constant initializers that write the buffer in wider pieces keep that form (`v1._0_4_ = ...`). Flip OFF to see the frame layout without the walk extent, for a bisect or an ablation.
- **Where / provenance:** P6/stack-frame-layout · kuna · structure-recovery · GH-468
- **Example:** `option endptrbound off`

### `arraysize` -- off | on | calls, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** a local char buffer is declared 8 bytes longer than the length passed to fgets/snprintf/read with it, e.g. char v3 [8200] beside fgets(v3,0x2000,fp); a stack array's size is a multiple of 16 plus 8 and it ends where the stack-protector canary slot starts; a buffer passed to __snprintf_chk(buf, n, 1, 0x100, ...) is declared longer than the 0x100 object size the call carries.
- **What it does:** End an escaped stack buffer at the byte count its calls state for it instead of at the next frame object. `ScopeLocal::restructure` (varmap.cc:1294) ends an open range where the next hint starts, and the compiler aligns a buffer of 16 bytes or more to 16, so the gap includes the padding before the next object: `char buf[8192]` below the stack-protector guard prints as `char buf[8200]`, `char buf[1001]` as `char buf[1016]`. `on`: each call that receives the exact start of the buffer states a constant byte count for it: a length a library function may fill (`fgets`, `snprintf`, `read`, `readlink`, `strftime`, `getcwd`, `fread`'s size times count), a length it writes exactly or only reads (`memset`, a `memcpy` source, `write`), or the destination object size of a `_FORTIFY_SOURCE` `__*_chk` call; a call that returns how many bytes it stored states one byte more when the function writes one byte at that result on every path (`n = readlink(p, buf, 4096); buf[n] = 0;`). The open range ends at the largest fill length or object size when no count comes within one byte of the gap, the count is at least 16 bytes, a whole number of elements, at most 15 bytes short of the gap (the padding a 16-byte alignment can leave) and at least every other count and every hint the range absorbed, and every access the function makes through the buffer is bounded inside it: no index other than such a terminator near its start, no loop that walks a pointer through it, no library call given it with a non-constant length that is not a byte-count result, no constant-offset access past the count. A fill length one byte short of a multiple of 16 (`readlink(p, buf, sizeof buf - 1)`) keeps that byte; an object size never moves. The bytes past the array stay unmapped, as alignment padding does. `calls` also takes any constant argument of any other call that receives the buffer's start (`ftoastr(buf, 0x1f, ..)`, `nstrftime(buf, 0x3e9, ..)`), which is a guess about what the callee does with it. `off` keeps upstream's gap.
- **When to flip:** On by default. The tell it fixes is a local `char` buffer declared 1 to 15 bytes longer than the length every call passes with it (`char v3 [8200];` beside `fgets(v3,0x2000,fp)`), the extra bytes being the alignment padding up to the next local or the stack guard. Flip `off` to see the frame gap upstream assigns. Known guesses `on` makes: a function that passes a shorter length than its buffer (`fgets(buf, 20, fp)` into a 24-byte array) is declared at that length; a stack structure whose first member is a `char` array filled by a library call (at `_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2` the `str*`/`printf`/`fgets` object size is the member's) is declared as that member; a terminator written after the result was capped by a comparison still adds its byte. `calls` also sizes buffers passed with a constant to the binary's own functions (`umaxtostr`-style helpers take no length and stay as they are); it is off by default because a constant beside a buffer need not be its length, and on ARM firmware it shrinks buffers below their size.
- **Where / provenance:** P6/stack-frame-layout · kuna · type-inference · ty17-stack-array-size
- **Example:** `option arraysize off`

### `castobject` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** an out-parameter local is passed as (int *)&v2 to waitpid or wait; a stack local is declared unsigned int where the callee that fills it declares int *; return (int)v1 >> 8 & 0xff; over an unsigned int status filled by waitpid.
- **What it does:** Declare a stack local whose address only fills declared `int *`-style parameters at the pointee the callee declares, when no reader wants the other signedness: `int v5; waitpid(v2,&v5,0)` instead of `unsigned int v5; waitpid(v2,(int *)&v5,0)`.
