Missing or ambiguous proof leaves the switch unresolved. This option changes only the discovery Listing; the independent xrefs table policy is unchanged.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/code-data-partition · kuna · new-analysis · GH-299
- **Example:** `--option listing on --option fast_funcdisc off --option aif on --option x86listingswitch on`

### `aifpoolslide` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** a sub_ entry starts on a literal pool word one word before a real function; a stripped arm function list lists a function 4 bytes early; a function's first decoded instruction is a conditional addvs or a movs r0,#0 that no code reaches; a real arm function is missing from a stripped inventory while the entry just before it is a pool word; aif adds entries on literal pools.
- **What it does:** Never plant an Aggressive Instruction Finder gap entry on a literal-pool word; plant it on the code after the pool (GH-299). ARM code keeps its constants in pools right after the code that loads them, so a pool usually sits between one function and the next, and the Listing walk never decodes it. The gap walk reads a pool word as an instruction (an A32 image address 0x608xxxxx as addvs, the high half of a Thumb SRAM pointer 0x2000xxxx as movs r0,#0) whose pairing with the next function's prologue matches the fingerprint, and whose speculative body runs into that function and validates; the entry lands a word or half a word early and, because an accept consumes its body, the function behind it is never probed. With this on, the walk keeps the set of words that ldr and vldr instructions load PC-relatively (their absolute [0x...] operand or [pc,#imm] form, both words of a 64-bit load; adr only takes an address and does not count), from the decoded Listing and from every body it accepts or consumes. A candidate inside a run of adjacent such words is probed as before, but its accept is planted on the first address after the run when its body decoded an instruction there, and it is rejected otherwise so the walk reaches the code after the pool. When that address is data (bytes that begin a printable NUL-terminated string, or an even address some literal word of Thumb code holds) the candidate is refused but still consumes its body, so bogus literal words decoded from a string table never move an entry onto a string; a bracket refusal also keeps consuming its body. 32-bit ARM only. Measured with each stripped image scored against its unstripped twin's symbol table, default mode: over the 93 non-u-boot 32-bit ARM ELFs of the decbench corpus mid-body entries fall 4,375 to 1,866 net and true function starts rise by 222; on the two u-boot A32 images mid-body entries fall 1,415 to 1,081 and true starts rise by 334; no true start is lost, and CMSIS_DAP.axf, 12 i386 decbench PEs, 17 Wine DLLs, 16 MinGW crackmes and 25 x86-64 images are unchanged. Besides the 556 true starts the new entries are 5 mid-body entries and 63 on data, none on a string start, against 88 data entries removed. Like poolentry it moves a function four bytes in when a literal reference resolves onto the function's own first word, which the gap walk without it gets right in --mode reliable; the corpus has no such case. Inert without aif and without --option listing on, so the datatest corpus is byte-identical.
- **When to flip:** On (default). It only moves or refuses a gap entry whose first bytes some instruction loads as a constant, so it removes entries that are data and lists the function behind the pool at its own address. Flip off to reproduce the GH-299 measurement exactly, or when an ARM image computes into a word it also executes (self-modifying code) and a real function that begins on a loaded word disappears from a stripped function list.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/code-data-partition · kuna · correctness-fix · GH-299
- **Example:** `--option aifpoolslide off`

### `tailcallentry` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** routine reached only by a tail B produces no decompiled output at all; a shared ISR handler is swallowed by the two-instruction stub that branches to it; function entry missing where the previous function ends in an unconditional branch; kuna emits one oversized function where the ground truth has two.
- **What it does:** On an ARM image, recover the function entries the recursive-descent Listing walk absorbs at a tail call. walk.rs makes a new function only at a CALL target and treats every other flow target as a same-function successor, so a routine reached only by a tail `B` is swallowed by whichever function branched to it and never becomes a function of its own — 17.4% of the ARM Cortex-M entry-recall gap. This reads the COMPLETED walk (splitting at a tail call provably cannot change which instructions the walk decodes, because a function entry is walked and therefore decoded either way) and admits an unconditional-branch target as a NEW function entry when four containment guards hold: every predecessor of the target is an unconditional branch (no fall-through and no conditional-branch predecessor, which would make it ordinary intra-function flow); the branch leaves the caller's entry-ordered function region, so at least one other discovered entry lies between the branch and its target; the target's flow region reaches a RETURN or computed jump (terminating-routine validity, with no length floor, so a one-instruction `bx lr` handler qualifies); and the target does not open with a stack restore (a function does not begin by tearing down a frame it never built — that is the caller's shared epilogue). Emits the accepted targets as the existing entries fact and never rebuilds the Listing, so no already-discovered entry can be removed. ARM-only; requires the Listing (option listing on) — a no-op when the Listing is absent, so every parity gate is byte-identical.
- **When to flip:** On by default, with `listing` (which `kuna decompile`, `decompile-all` and `functions` inject on non-x86-64 and the `aggressive` preset supplies): on stripped ARM firmware a routine reached only by a tail `B` -- a shared ISR stub's handler, a `pop {r4,lr} ; b helper` tail call, a jump-thunk target -- becomes a function of its own instead of being absorbed into an earlier function and producing no output. Measured on 96 Cortex-M images: +561 ground-truth functions, 94.6% of the new entries are real function starts, zero real bodies split, zero entries lost. Inert on every non-ARM image and without `listing`. Flip off to leave the walk's absorption in place.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/code-data-partition · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-analysis-tailcallentry
- **Example:** `option listing on --option tailcallentry on`

### `goabi` -- auto | off, default `auto`

- **Symptoms:** go function parameters missing or void while the body reads rax/rbx locals that are never assigned; a go function returning two values loses the second and the statements computing it; go output full of unassigned register-commented locals; multi-return go call sites read registers the call never defines.
- **What it does:** Select the vendored golang compiler spec for a Go image. Go does not use the platform C ABI: since 1.17 its register ABI (abi-internal) passes arguments in RAX,RBX,RCX,RDI,RSI,R8-R11 on x86-64 and returns multiple values in those same registers, so under the default gcc model a Go function's parameters are invisible (RAX/RBX are scratch to SysV), a second return value is dead-coded away, and the statements computing it are DELETED - `func pair(a,b int) (int,int)` decompiles as `long pair(void){ return v1 + v2; }` with both locals unassigned and the product gone. Ghidra vendors golang cspecs (abi-internal default, abi0 the stack ABI, the write-barrier and duff helper models) for x86-64, x86-32 and AArch64; kuna ships them compiled and nothing selected them. At `auto` (default) an image whose effective source language is Go (the sourcelang fact, KUNA_SOURCELANG force included) composes the `:golang` compiler field in its SLEIGH language id on those three little-endian architectures; every other architecture and every non-Go image is untouched, and the engine's default-model retry covers a spec that fails to resolve. The id is composed inside `load file`, so the option travels as the KUNA_GOABI environment variable (the rexthunk/sourcelang loadtime pattern). The golang cspec also registers the `abi0` stack-ABI model, and a function or callee whose name ends `.abi0` (Go's dual-ABI stack alias - an unstripped go1.22 hello-world carries 115 such .symtab names; the pclntab carries none, so a stripped image keeps abi-internal everywhere) takes that model at the model-selection seams; the binding self-gates on the model being registered, so an explicit `--target ...:golang` gets it even with goabi off.
- **When to flip:** Leave auto: on a Go binary the golang cspec is the difference between invisible parameters with deleted statements and recovered register arguments with the multi-return join; flip off to read a Go image under the platform C model (comparing against another tool, or triaging a suspected cspec defect). Non-Go binaries never see the option either way.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/environment-binding · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-multilang-goabi
- **Example:** `option goabi off`

### `gotypeglobals` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** go decompile shows runtime.newobject(&DAT_...) or convT(&DAT_...) with no hint which type is allocated; interface conversion call sites in go output pass anonymous dat_ globals; go:itab interface-dispatch tables render as bare &DAT_ addresses instead of go:itab.<concrete>,<interface>; runtime functions walking type descriptors render raw offset arithmetic instead of named fields; harvested go struct names exist in the type catalog but never appear in any function's C.
- **What it does:** Name and type a Go image's `_type` descriptors as data globals - the first consumer of the gotypes runtime-type harvest. A Go binary's runtime metadata types two families of data objects outright: its own `_type` descriptors and the interface-dispatch tables (itabs) that bind them. A descriptor is a global of layout internal/abi.Type that Go's linker names `type:main.Point` / `type:*main.Point` / `type:[]uint8`. Stripping deletes those symtab names but the records stay reachable through the moduledata, so every allocation and interface-conversion site - `runtime.newobject(&type:main.Point)`, convT*, assertE, mapiterinit - decompiles as a call on a bare `&DAT_...` constant and the recovered named types never appear in the C. With the option on, every descriptor the gotypes walk decodes (typelinks or the go1.26+ descriptor region, pointer pointees included) is committed as a data symbol at the record's VMA: the linker-spelling `type:<name>` name, the `go.typedesc` shell (the 48/32-byte abi.Type base record, so runtime code walking a descriptor renders named field reads like `t->Kind_`), typelock|namelock at the engine's typed-data seam. The same walk names each static itab the moduledata lists - the go1.18..1.25 `itablinks` pointer slice or the go1.26+ `[types + itaboffset, + itabsize)` region walked by each record's `ITab.Size()` - as a name-only `go:itab.<concrete>,<interface>` data symbol, its two type names built from the two descriptor ADDRESSES the itab record points at (offsets 0 and 8), never a spelled name; so an interface conversion renders `go:itab.main.Point,fmt.Stringer` instead of a bare `&DAT_...`. The itab symbol is a NAME, not a typed object (an itab address is used polymorphically - passed to getitab, compared, stored into an interface word - so locking its global to a struct type would demote those uses and hide the very symbol a reference renders, exactly how Go's own symtab names an itab untyped), and an itab the image already names (an unstripped binary's symbol table) is left to that name, so the pass only ever ADDS the itabs stripping removed. Names that cannot print safely (anonymous `struct { ... }` literals, `func(int) bool` - anything with interior whitespace) are dropped; unnamed composite spellings (`[]uint8`, `map[string]int`) are kept, they are what an analyst searches for. The facts are produced at load and the COMMIT is gated, so `off` renders exactly what the gotypes provider alone renders; non-Go images produce no facts and never see the option.
- **When to flip:** On by default: on a Go binary every runtime.newobject/convT/assertE call site names the type it manipulates instead of a bare &DAT_ constant, which is how the harvested named types become visible in decompiled C at all. Flip off to compare against the bare-metadata rendering (triaging whether a wrong name came from the descriptor walk) or to keep the symbol table minimal on a huge Go image. Non-Go binaries are byte-identical either way.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/code-data-partition · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-multilang-gotypeglobals
- **Example:** `option gotypeglobals off`

### `dyldimage` -- none | <install-name>, default `none`

- **Symptoms:** a dyld_shared_cache file is rejected as an unrecognized input format; cannot decompile an ios or macos system library because it only exists inside the dyld shared cache; dyld shared cache holds N images; choose one with --image.
- **What it does:** Choose which image of a dyld shared cache to load. A cache (dyld_shared_cache_arm64e and its sub-caches .01, .27.dylddata, .44.dyldlinkedit, ... and .symbols beside it) holds every system library of an iOS or macOS release; kuna rebuilds the chosen image as a standalone thin Mach-O before anything parses it, so the loader, the analysis passes and every surface see an ordinary Mach-O. The rebuild keeps each segment at its cache address, applies the cache's slide info (v2, v3 with arm64e auth pointers, v5) at slide zero so every rebased pointer reads as its unslid target, and gives the image a private __LINKEDIT with its own symbol table, the local symbols the cache moved to its .symbols file in place of the <redacted> placeholders, the renumbered indirect-symbol table, and copies of the export trie, function starts and data-in-code. The name matches a full install name (/usr/lib/libobjc.A.dylib), else a unique basename (libobjc.A.dylib, CoreFoundation), else a unique basename without its last extension (libobjc.A). `none` (default) loads the image of a one-image cache and refuses a larger one with the image count. The image is rebuilt inside `load file`, so the choice travels as the KUNA_DYLD_IMAGE environment variable; the CLI's global `--image NAME` sets it for every subcommand, and the console sets it with `option dyldimage NAME` before `load file`, accepted before any image is loaded. `kuna unpack <cache> --list` lists the images and `kuna unpack <cache> --image NAME` writes the rebuilt Mach-O.
- **When to flip:** Set it (or pass --image) whenever the input is a dyld shared cache: kuna decompile dyld_shared_cache_arm64e --image CoreFoundation CFStringCreateCopy. Not used for any other input.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/environment-binding · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-apple-dyldcache
- **Example:** `option dyldimage /usr/lib/libobjc.A.dylib`

### `dyldcrossrefs` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** calls in a dyld shared cache image render as sub_<addr> into a __TEXT_STUBS island; a cache image's __got loads name nothing; cross-library calls of an ios framework have no names.
- **What it does:** Name the calls and GOT loads a dyld shared cache image makes into other images. The cache builder routes most cross-image calls past the image's own stubs: on iOS 16 a bl lands on a stub island in a __TEXT_STUBS sub-cache (adrp x16; add x16; br x16 to the callee), on iOS 14 on another image's rewritten stub, and within branch range on the callee itself. It also coalesces __got sections and drops their indirect-symbol entries. None of those targets is inside the rebuilt image, so a call renders as sub_<island address>(...) and a load through a coalesced slot names nothing. When the image is rebuilt, kuna finds every branch target outside it and every coalesced GOT slot pointing outside it. It follows a stub (adrp/add/ldr then br, braa or braaz) to its final target and names that target from the symbol table of the image holding it: exports first, then the locals in the .symbols file. The table rides in the rebuilt Mach-O as a kuna.dyld.xrefs LC_NOTE, and the Mach-O import walk reads it back, so each island becomes a named import stub and each slot a named import slot. Read inside `load file`, so the gate travels as the KUNA_DYLDCROSSREFS environment variable. Inert on every input that is not a rebuilt cache image.
- **When to flip:** Leave on: CoreFoundation's 9,136 calls into stub islands render as __stack_chk_fail(), os_unfair_lock_lock_with_options(...) instead of sub_18c99b570(). Turn off to see the raw island addresses, for example to check a call against the cache's island layout.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/environment-binding · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-apple-dyldcache
- **Example:** `option dyldcrossrefs off`

### `sourcelang` -- auto | c | rust | go | swift, default `auto`

- **Symptoms:** rust binary renders with c output and no rust abi handling because a stripped image lost its language signals; a c binary is detected as another language and language-gated rules misfire; go runtime passes do not run on a go binary whose buildinfo section was stripped.
- **What it does:** Override the detected source language of the image. kuna detects what produced a binary once at load (the port of Ghidra's SourceLanguageAnalyzer: Go build-info sections - on a Windows PE, which has none, a build-info blob that validates at the head of .data together with a pclntab in read-only data - rustc .comment records / mangled symbols / .rodata signatures, Swift metadata sections / mangled symbols / runtime imports, else the C toolchain conveniences) and that verdict is a single stored fact consumed everywhere language matters: analysis-pass selection inside `load file` (the Go pclntab pass, the Rust/Go no-return widening), the engine-plane Architecture::source_lang that per-function rules gate on (`rustabi auto`, `reloadarg`'s Go stand-down), and the output-language auto policy. `auto` (default) trusts detection; `c`, `rust`, `go` and `swift` force the verdict for all of those consumers at once. Because pass selection happens inside `load file`, upstream of every per-function option command, the forced value travels as the KUNA_SOURCELANG environment variable set by the CLI before loading (the rexthunk/relocobjects loadtime pattern); the console `option sourcelang` arm updates the engine fact for the already-loaded program and bridges the env for a later `load file` in the same process. Forcing a language never invents facts a binary lacks (forcing `go` on a non-Go image enables the pclntab pass, which then simply finds no table); what it reliably changes is which language-gated rules may act. A `cpp` value is deliberately absent until something consumes a C-vs-C++ distinction.
- **When to flip:** Force `c` when detection claims the wrong language (a C image embedding Rust-looking strings or a `$s`-prefixed symbol) and language-gated rules are misfiring; force `rust`/`go`/`swift` on a stripped or post-processed binary whose language signals were removed (no .comment record, sections renamed) so the language passes act anyway. Leave `auto` otherwise - detection is high-precision by construction.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/environment-binding · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-multilang-sourcelang
- **Example:** `option sourcelang rust`

### `lazyfuncs` -- on | off, default `off`

- **Symptoms:** kuna decompile on a large c++ .so needs ~750 MB for one function; read symbols dominates a single-function run on an entry-dense image.
- **What it does:** Commit the analysis tier's discovered entry points as NAMES only and build a Function where the decompiler reads one, instead of one per entry at `read symbols`. A dense .eh_frame reports every function as an entry (377,429 on a 51 MB Android .so) at ~0.84 KB each -- 315 MB of a single-function run's peak that the run never reads.
- **When to flip:** Off (default) is Ghidra's whole-inventory commit. On builds a Function only for the selection and for what its p-code reads (call and tail targets, code addresses taken as values): `kuna decompile <big c++ .so> <fn>` drops 30-38% of peak and 33-42% of the time on entry-dense images, byte-identical over 102 sampled functions across six images. Gains track entry density (a Go binary moves 2%); a whole-binary surface still materializes everything it walks.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/code-data-partition · kuna · speed · kuna-lazyfuncs
- **Example:** `option lazyfuncs on`

### `objc` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** objective-c methods render as sub_<addr> instead of -[Class sel]; __objc_ metadata present but classes and selectors unnamed in a mach-o; a message send renders as sub_<addr>(obj) through an __objc_stubs entry; objc_msgSend selector argument renders as dat_<addr>; a category method renders as sub_<addr> instead of -[Class(Category) sel].
- **What it does:** On a Mach-O, run the Objective-C metadata recovery pass: walk the __objc_* ObjC 2.0 metadata web (the kuna analog of Ghidra's ObjcTypeMetadataAnalyzer, name-recovery half). From __objc_classlist (array of class_t*), per class follow data & FAST_DATA_MASK (~0x7) to the class_ro_t, read .name (class name) and .baseMethods (the - instance method_list_t), and follow class_t.isa to the metaclass baseMethods (the + class methods). Walk method_list_t handling BOTH the large absolute-pointer form and the small/relative form (entsizeAndFlags & 0x80000000), per method_t resolving the selector (ASCII), type encoding, and IMP (function VA). RENAME each IMP function -[Class sel] / +[Class sel] — but only when it still carries an engine FUN_*/sub_* placeholder (the label gate, the FID precedent; a real symbol is never overwritten) — plus emit _OBJC_CLASS_$_<name> + selector symbols. Selectors are plain ASCII, so no demangler is needed. Also walks `__objc_catlist`/`__objc_nlcatlist` and renames each category method `-[Class(Category) sel]` (the class read off its class_t, or off the import name when the category extends a class from another image), walks `__objc_protolist` and names each protocol_t `_OBJC_PROTOCOL_$_<P>` while recording its methods' type encodings (a selector this image only declares in a protocol still types its `objc_msgSend$<sel>` stub), and names the reference slots code actually loads from — `selRef_<sel>` for __objc_selrefs, `classRef_<Class>` / `superRef_<Class>` for __objc_classrefs / __objc_superrefs, `protoRef_<P>` for __objc_protorefs (a bind slot is named from its chained import or classic LC_DYLD_INFO bind program) — and each `__objc_stubs` entry as the function `objc_msgSend$<sel>` it is the linker's stub for, so a send through a stub renders `objc_msgSend$init(obj)` instead of `sub_<addr>(obj)`. Each ivar offset variable in __objc_ivar is the 4-byte data object `<Class>::<ivar>`. Registered ONLY for a Mach-O binary, so it is a structural no-op on every non-Mach-O target. arm64 and x86-64; chained fixups (LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS) are resolved. DISABLED in the shipped catalog (output-changing: renames IMP functions + adds symbols; real-binary-path only, so every parity gate is byte-identical), but ON in the `aggressive` preset, which `auto` selects for any binary under 500 KiB, so on a Mach-O image of that size it runs without being asked for. The rebase reference slots are also painted read-only and foldable (dyld writes them once, before any code runs), so a load through a selref/classref/superref folds to the selector or class it holds — `objc_msgSend(obj, sel_init)` rather than `objc_msgSend(obj, selRef_init)`; a bind slot has no static value and keeps its name (formerly the objcrefconst option).
- **When to flip:** On by default: a Mach-O Objective-C binary gets its method names recovered -- a stripped IMP renders -[Greeter greet:] instead of sub_<addr>, the class/selector strings and the selector/class reference slots are named, and a send through an `__objc_stubs` entry renders `objc_msgSend$<sel>(obj, ...)`; `objcrefconst` (on by default) then folds the reference slots to what they hold. Inert on every non-Mach-O image and on a Mach-O with no __objc_classlist. Flip off to keep the engine placeholders.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/external-refinement · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-analysis-objc
- **Example:** `option objc on`

### `objcsdk` -- <directory> | off, default `off`

- **Symptoms:** objc_msgSend$setFoo:() renders with no argument although the caller sets one; objc_msgSend$setAlpha: shows 0x3ff0000000000000 instead of 1.0; objc_msgSend$setFrame: passes one word where a CGRect was built; a framework method's stub returns undefined16 or unsigned long instead of its declared type.
- **What it does:** Read Objective-C method signatures from SDK headers for the selectors an image only sends. A selector stub `objc_msgSend$setAlpha:` gets a prototype only when something in the image declares the selector (a class, category or protocol of its own), so a send to a framework method kept the untyped call-site inference and lost its arguments (`objc_msgSend$setHidden:();`). The declarations exist in the SDK the app was built against, and Apple's headers are never shipped with kuna, so this names a directory to read at load: an SDK root (`.../iPhoneOS.sdk`) contributes the `Headers/` of every framework the image links (LC_LOAD_DYLIB), any other directory every `.h` under it. The reader takes the declaration subset of the grammar — `@interface`/`@protocol`/category bodies, `- (ret)sel:(T)a ...;` methods, `@property (attrs) T name;` with `getter=`/`setter=`/`readonly` honoured, `typedef`s so NSInteger, CGFloat, NS_ENUM names and NSString-backed typed enums resolve — and turns each into the type encoding the runtime metadata would carry (`v@:d`), which rides the existing selector-to-prototype path: scalars and pointers pinned to their x/d registers, an HFA struct such as CGRect spread over d0..d3 as `arg_x, arg_y, arg_width, arg_height`, NSRange over two x registers, a larger struct (CGAffineTransform) the pointer the caller passes, a struct return the flat struct the model places in d0..d3. A type the reader cannot encode (an unknown struct, a function pointer) makes the selector unusable rather than guessed; one selector declared two ways across classes is dropped (a differing class-pointer argument is not a disagreement). The image's own declarations always win over the headers. Load-time, env-bridged (KUNA_OBJCSDK): set it before the `load file` it should apply to; nothing derived from the headers is written anywhere.
- **When to flip:** Off (default): only the image's own metadata types a send. Point it at the SDK the app was built against (`--option objcsdk ~/sdks/iPhoneOS16.5.sdk`) to type every UIKit/Foundation send; on a 1.9 MB iOS app that takes argument-less stub calls from 2,897 to 1,221 of 25,084 and renders `objc_msgSend$setAlpha:(v, 1.0)`, `objc_msgSend$setFrame:(v, r.x, r.y, r.width, r.height)`. A directory of your own headers works the same way. Inert unless `objc` is on.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/external-refinement · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-analysis-objc
- **Example:** `option objcsdk /path/to/iPhoneOS.sdk`

### `swiftmetadata` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** swift binary functions render as sub_<addr> although swift5 metadata sections are present; type metadata accessors unnamed in a stripped swift mach-o; protocol witnesses and class methods of a stripped swift app have no names.
- **What it does:** On a Swift-built Mach-O or ELF, run the runtime-metadata recovery pass: read the swift5_* reflection sections a stripped Swift binary keeps (__swift5_types / swift5_type_metadata, the nominal type context descriptors; __swift5_protos, the protocol descriptors; __swift5_proto, the conformance descriptors; __swift5_fieldmd, the field descriptors) and name what they point at, in the demangler's name-only conventions so the names read like symbol-table names: each type's metadata accessor (Module.Type.type_metadata_accessor), each class vtable slot's implementation by position and kind (Module.Class.vtable#3.getter - the slot carries no selector), each override whose overridden method descriptor is an import (Module.Sub.viewDidLoad(), the real member name, read from the …Tq import the override table points at), each resilient protocol witness (<Module.Type:Swift.Hashable>.hash(into:) when the requirement descriptor is an import, <T:P>.requirement#2 for a local protocol, Module.P.requirement#2.default for a default implementation), and the records themselves (….nominal_type_descriptor, ….protocol_descriptor, ….module_descriptor, <T:P>.protocol_conformance_descriptor, <T:P>.protocol_witness_table, ….reflection_field_descriptor). Type paths follow the parent chain (Module.Outer.Inner; a private/anonymous context is transparent; an extension context demangles its extended type; a parent in another image is named through its module-descriptor import). Function names use the FID-precedent label-gated rename: a real symbol is never overwritten, only an engine sub_*/FUN_* placeholder. Everything in the sections is 32-bit self-relative, so no fixup resolution is needed except for indirect references, which go through the chained-fixup overlay (rebases) or the import table (binds); a record the reader cannot follow is skipped, never guessed. Registered for Mach-O and ELF (the formats Swift ships in) when the loader detected a Swift image; an image without the sections produces nothing, so every other binary is byte-identical.
- **When to flip:** On by default: a stripped Swift binary's metadata accessors, class vtable implementations, overrides of imported methods and protocol witnesses render under their type's path instead of sub_<addr>, and the descriptor records are named. Inert on every image the loader did not detect as Swift and on any image without swift5_* sections. Flip off to keep the sub_<addr> placeholders.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/external-refinement · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-analysis-swiftmetadata
- **Example:** `option swiftmetadata on`

### `cfstrings` -- on | off | annotate, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** core-foundation / objc string constants render as dat_<addr> instead of their text; a CFSTR(...) argument shows an address in a mach-o.
- **What it does:** Run the Mach-O Core Foundation constant-string recovery pass: when the binary is a Mach-O, read each __cfstring entry (the four-word CFString struct isa/flags/data-pointer/length), resolve its data pointer through the LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS overlay on an arm64(e) image (a raw word on a classic LC_DYLD_INFO image), read the string (8-bit when the flags unicode bit 0x10 is clear, UTF-16 decoded to UTF-8 when set), and render a reference to the entry as the string literal. The commit seam types each entry a typelocked opaque struct __CFString symbol, whose pointer the type factory spells CFStringRef (so a function returning or passing the entry is typed CFStringRef), and pre-seeds the StringManager at the entry address with the resolved bytes, so a CFSTR argument renders as CFSTR("text") instead of dat_<addr> (the C printer wraps the literal in CFSTR(...) because the value is the CFStringRef entry, not its characters; annotate also follows it with a /* cfstring@0x<entry> */ comment naming the entry address a listing or hex view shows) -- the same route that renders a __cstring literal, carried across the CFString struct indirection the printer cannot follow on its own. The entry structs are marked read-only (a CFString constant is immutable), which the constant-string route requires on the historical writable __DATA,__cfstring layout (__DATA_CONST is already read-only). Registered ONLY for a Mach-O binary, so it is a structural no-op on every non-Mach-O target. ENABLED by default: Mach-O-only and real-binary-path only, so the XML datatest corpus never runs it (0/675 assertions moved); on an 80 MB third-party arm64 iOS app a decompile is within noise of off (min 2.324 s off vs 2.359 s on, medians 2.442 / 2.372 s over 6 interleaved runs).
- **When to flip:** On (default): a Mach-O (Core Foundation / Objective-C / Swift) binary renders its CFString constants -- a call that passed dat_<addr> renders CFSTR("cfstring hello"). Flip off to see each reference as the __cfstring entry itself (its symbol, or its address on a stripped image). Use annotate when cross-checking against a disassembler or hex view: the entry address stays in the output as a comment.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/external-refinement · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-analysis-cfstrings
- **Example:** `option cfstrings annotate`

### `swifttypes` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** swift struct and class fields render as raw offsets off self; swift getters named by swiftmetadata take no self parameter; type metadata accessors return undefined16.
- **What it does:** The type-layout arm of the Swift metadata pass (inert unless swiftmetadata is on): a non-generic type whose metadata needs no runtime initialization has it laid out statically, and its accessor is the one-line function that returns the address (adrp/add on arm64, lea on x86-64; a class with Objective-C heritage tail-calls the runtime with the same address). From that metadata the pass reads a struct's size and alignment (its value witness table, or the builtin table an import names) and its 32-bit field offset vector, a class's instance size and pointer-sized field offset vector; from the reflection field descriptor each stored property's name and mangled type, whose symbolic references the descriptor table resolves. The result is one kuna struct per type under its dotted name (Module.Point { long x; long y; }; a class as its object layout, a local superclass embedded as super, an imported one leaving the isa word) with field types mapped from the Swift type (Int/UInt/Double/Float/Bool and their sized forms, Swift.String as its two words, a class reference as a pointer to that class's struct, a nested struct inline, a collection as its storage word, a closure as its two words) and undefined<n> for any other (an enum, an imported value type, a generic instantiation) over the bytes up to the next field. Also typed: the metadata records (….type_metadata / ….class_metadata, ….value_witness_table), the accessors (swift.type_metadata *Module.Type.type_metadata_accessor(long request)), and the self of every class vtable getter and local-protocol witness getter (Class ** for a class witness, Class * under a class-bound protocol), which Swift passes in the swiftself register (x20 / r13) that no calling-convention model describes - pinned on the function as a register-locked parameter, the rest of the signature recovered as usual. A type whose dotted path two descriptors share, whose field count disagrees with its descriptor, or whose offsets overlap is given no layout. Default-ON because it is inert unless swiftmetadata is on (default-off, but ON in the `aggressive` preset, which `auto` selects for any binary under 500 KiB, so this arm runs with no flags on small Swift binaries) and adds about 0.1 s and 3 MB on an 84 MB app.
- **When to flip:** Off only to see a swiftmetadata-named binary without layouts: fields render as raw offsets, getters take no self, the accessors return undefined16. On (default) when swiftmetadata is on: self->field through the recovered struct, typed metadata records.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/external-refinement · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-analysis-swifttypes
- **Example:** `option swifttypes off`

### `swiftcall` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** swift methods named by swiftmetadata read self from an unnamed x20 or r13; calls to swift methods drop the self they pass; a try? error path or a do/catch after a throwing call folds away; swift struct mutating methods write through an untyped register.
- **What it does:** The calling-convention arm of the Swift metadata pass (inert unless swiftmetadata is on; it reads the type-layout arm, so swifttypes off turns it off too). Swift passes a method's self in the swiftself register (x20 on arm64, r13 on x86-64) when it is one pointer - a class instance, the address of a mutating or indirect value, a thick metatype - and returns a throwing function's error in the swifterror register (x21 / r12), which the caller zeroes before the call and tests after it. Under the C model neither register is a parameter, so a method's self is an unnamed register read, a call drops the self it passes, and the caller's test reads the zero it stored, so the error path of try? folds away. Every AArch64 and x86-64 compiler spec gains __swiftcall (its default model with swiftself as an input resource section of its own, so self is a parameter exactly when the body reads it and never forces the argument registers around it) and __swiftcall_throws (the same, handing the error register back to the caller), derived when the spec is read unless it declares models of those names, so they need no edit to the vendored specs and a spec a Ghidra host sends carries them too. The arm binds __swiftcall to every function it can place in a type, with no signature so the arity stays recovered: a class's vtable slots and overrides, a conformance's witnesses, a protocol's default implementations, and in an image that kept its symbols each method, accessor, initializer and deinitializer the demangler places in a class, struct or enum (throws read off the function type selects __swiftcall_throws; a struct's static member, whose metatype is thin, takes none). Its self is named and, where the type is known, typed as an unlocked hint the recovered parameter takes: Class * for an instance member, swift.class_metadata * for a class member or allocating initializer, the address of the value for a witness (T * for a struct, Class ** for a class, the reference itself under a class-bound protocol), swift.type_metadata * for a static requirement; a body two types share (identical code folding) keeps the name and drops the type. A direct call to a bound function recovers its arguments under the model, so it passes self; a call to a struct member, which may take self exploded into its trailing arguments instead, keeps a swiftself argument only when the caller set the register after its last call that may read it (a runtime helper with a C name, such as swift_retain, preserves the register and reads none of it). A method's own self handed on untouched (x20 / r13 never rewritten) is passed at a direct call, and an indirect call passes swiftself exactly when its target is loaded through the isa of the value the register holds (obj->isa[k](obj, ...)), so a virtual call on an object shows that object and a value-witness call shows none. Any call, direct or indirect, whose block zeroes the error register as its last write before it and whose next read of the register compares it with zero is given __swiftcall_throws, so the test after it reads the callee's error; a register zeroed for its own sake and read back as a value keeps its value. Default-ON because it is inert unless swiftmetadata is on (default-off, but ON in the `aggressive` preset, which `auto` selects for any binary under 500 KiB, so this arm runs with no flags on small Swift binaries), the XML corpus never runs the pass (0/675), and on a large third-party iOS app (84 MB) the arm adds no measurable load time and about 8 MB, and decompiling the 42,240 functions it binds takes 2.5% longer (1:13:53 against 1:12:07).
- **When to flip:** Off to see a swiftmetadata-named binary under the C model: methods without self, calls without the self they pass, and try? error paths folded away. On (default) when swiftmetadata is on: self typed in methods, initializers, accessors and witnesses, passed at direct calls, and the error a throwing call returns tested where the binary tests it.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/external-refinement · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-analysis-swiftcall
- **Example:** `option swiftcall off`

### `pdb` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** stripped windows pe functions stay FUN_<addr> although a matching .pdb exists; pdb symbol names not applied to a pe; a .pdb beside the exe is ignored; windows function names need kuna_pdb_path to be set by hand.
- **What it does:** Run the PE PDB (Program Database) metadata recovery pass: on a Windows PE, recover function names from the external .pdb debug file (the kuna analog of Ghidra's PdbUniversalAnalyzer, name-recovery half). PDB is Windows' DWARF, but the debug info lives in a SEPARATE .pdb file the PE only fingerprints. Read the PE CodeView debug record ({guid|sig, age, .pdb path}), then LOCATE the .pdb through an ordered candidate list: (1) an explicit path in the kuna_pdb_path environment variable (the s1_fid kuna_fid_db external-artifact precedent), (2) the CodeView record's own filename resolved beside the image — the recorded string is build-machine content, so only its last path segment is used and only inside the image's own directory, never opened as a path — and (3) <image stem>.pdb beside the image. Each candidate passes the FINGERPRINT GATE: open it via the `pdb` crate and verify its pdb_information().guid/age matches the PE's CodeView record. The first match wins; a MISMATCH or unreadable candidate moves on (with one stderr line naming it, so a stale sidecar is not silently indistinguishable from no sidecar) and an exhausted list emits nothing — never apply a wrong/stale PDB (the FID full-hash-match discipline of never applying wrong external knowledge). On a match, walk the global symbol stream (S_PUB32 publics + S_GPROC32 procedures), resolve each to its VMA (segment:offset -> RVA + the PE ImageBase), and RENAME each stripped function to its real name — but only when it still carries an engine FUN_*/sub_* placeholder (the label gate, the FID precedent; a real symbol is never overwritten). Registered ONLY for a PE binary, so it is a structural no-op on every non-PE target. NAME-level only (stripped FUN_<addr> -> the real name); typed prototypes, typed stack locals, and source lines are deferred. ENABLED by default (DIV-129): the fingerprint gate makes the automatic search safe by construction, so every /Zi Windows build decompiles with its real names at zero configuration. Real-binary path only, so every parity gate is byte-identical.
- **When to flip:** On by default. A Windows PE built with /Zi (or clang -gcodeview) whose matching .pdb sits beside it recovers its real function names with no configuration; a PE with no .pdb on disk, or with one whose GUID/age does not match, is byte-identical to having the pass off. Set kuna_pdb_path to point at a .pdb that lives somewhere else (a symbol store, a build tree). Flip OFF to see the stripped FUN_<addr>/sub_<addr> names — a bisect, an ablation, or a check that a name came from the binary rather than from the sidecar.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/external-refinement · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-analysis-pdb
- **Example:** `option pdb off`

### `macho-arm64e` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** arm64e mach-o decoded with the generic v8A spec so pointer-auth ops are unmodeled; pac instructions in an apple-silicon binary not modeled by the loaded spec.
- **What it does:** On an arm64e Mach-O, select the Apple-Silicon pointer-authentication SLEIGH spec. A Mach-O whose header reports cpusubtype CPU_SUBTYPE_ARM64E loads with the AARCH64:LE:64:AppleSilicon language (the vendored Apple-Silicon v8.5-A spec, which models the pointer-auth/AMX extensions) instead of the generic AARCH64:LE:64:v8A. Pointer authentication does NOT change import naming or symbols (the __stubs indirect-symbol walk is unaffected) — only the spec selection differs (design 3.7). Spec selection is a LOAD-time decision (language_id_for), which runs before any console `option` command, so the live gate is the KUNA_MACHO_ARM64E env var: the kuna CLI exports it for `--option macho-arm64e off`, the console `option` arm sets it for a later `load file` in the same process, and this option name also records the requested state on the Architecture for catalog consistency. A non-arm64e Mach-O, a non-Mach-O target, and every ELF/PE/COFF path are byte-identical, so all parity gates are structurally untouched.
- **When to flip:** On by default: an arm64e (Apple-Silicon, pointer-auth) Mach-O decompiles under the AppleSilicon spec that models its extensions. Inert on every non-Mach-O image and on a Mach-O whose cpusubtype is not arm64e. Flip off to load an arm64e image with the generic v8A spec, exactly as any arm64.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/code-data-partition · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-multiformat-macho-arm64e
- **Example:** `--option macho-arm64e on`

### `kernelcache` -- auto | off | <bundle-id>, default `auto`

- **Symptoms:** an iOS kernelcache (IMG4/IM4P) is rejected as an unrecognized input format; kuna functions on a decompressed MH_FILESET kernelcache finds no functions; a kext cannot be selected out of a kernel collection; pointers in a kernelcache read as packed chained-fixup words instead of addresses.
- **What it does:** Load an Apple kernelcache straight from its firmware container. An IMG4 or bare IM4P file is parsed as DER, its payload is decoded (LZFSE bvx2/bvxn/bvx- blocks or a complzss LZSS container, checked against the declared size and Adler-32; decoding stops at the IM4P's declared size or at 64 times the payload, whichever is smaller, 16 MiB at least and never past 1 GiB), and an encrypted payload (one carrying a KBAG) is refused with a message instead of being misread. The decoded image is usually an MH_FILESET kernel collection: one Mach-O header per LC_FILESET_ENTRY (the kernel and every kext) sharing one file and one LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS table. kuna applies every rebase of that table to its pointer slot (DYLD_CHAINED_PTR_64_KERNEL_CACHE, ARM64E_KERNEL, ARM64E_FIRMWARE and X86_64_KERNEL_CACHE, pointer-authentication bits stripped) and then loads ONE entry as a thin Mach-O: `auto` takes the kernel (the MH_EXECUTE entry), a bundle id takes that entry, matched exactly or by a unique dotted suffix (`IOSurface` finds com.apple.iokit.IOSurface). Loader-tier: read through the KUNA_KERNELCACHE env var, because the image is chosen inside load file.
- **When to flip:** Auto (default): `kuna functions kernelcache` lists the kernel's functions with their symbol names; `--option kernelcache com.apple.iokit.IOSurface` loads that kext instead, its direct calls into the kernel named after the kernel functions they reach; `--option kernelcache list` stops with the list of every entry id. Flip off to pass the bytes through untouched: an IMG4 is then an unrecognized format and a bare MH_FILESET loads as one image with no code sections.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/code-data-partition · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-kernelcache
- **Example:** `--option kernelcache com.apple.iokit.IOSurface`

### `godwarfsig` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** go functions lose source parameters despite dwarf; go identity function decompiles as void; go result parameters appear as inputs.
- **What it does:** On an amd64 Go binary with DWARF, recover Go scalar and pointer function signatures from the compiler DWARF, including bounded zlib debug sections. Resolve cross-unit type references, separate result formals using DW_AT_variable_parameter, and verify complete contracts against the little-endian amd64 Go register ABI. Pointers may target grounded scalars or flat records. Decompression, type interning and address-bound prototype installation run only on such an image. Aggregates by value, unsupported multiple results, stack arguments, hidden-context functions and incomplete metadata retain existing inference. Exactly two full-width signed or unsigned integer results are recovered as well when the contract is complete (independent RAX/RBX result allocation, joined storage, a unique function entry): they are carried in an ordinary struct with validated language metadata and Go declarations, calls and returns use multiple-result syntax (formerly the gopairreturns option).
- **When to flip:** On by default: a Go binary with DWARF keeps its parameter names, pointer types and an identity function's return value. Requires the abi-internal compiler model (the Go cspec `goabi` selects) and little-endian amd64; stripped images, non-Go images and other architectures are unchanged. Flip off to leave the Go prototypes to inference.
- **Where / provenance:** P1/external-refinement · kuna · analysis-enablement · kuna-angr-go-dwarf-signatures
- **Example:** `option godwarfsig on`

## Core rendering defaults

Part of the decompiler; not the control surface. Flip only to reproduce upstream Ghidra output byte-for-byte or for unusual downstream consumers.

### `compareform` -- canonical | original, default `original`

- **Symptoms:** comparison constant off by one versus upstream ghidra (x <= 9 vs x < 10); need the analysis-canonical compare form to diff against upstream ghidra output.
- **What it does:** Whether comparisons keep their source form (V <= c) or the analysis-canonical rewrite (V < c+1).
- **When to flip:** Flip to canonical only to reproduce upstream Ghidra output; original (default) is more faithful to source.
- **Where / provenance:** P3/comparison-canonicalization · ghidra-upstream · presentation-default · GH-558
- **Example:** `option compareform canonical`

### `arraynotation` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** &base[index] rendering unwanted; consumer expects raw pointer arithmetic; indexed array form where base + offset arithmetic is desired for diffing.
- **What it does:** Render standalone pointer arithmetic as &base[index] (on) vs base + index (off).
- **When to flip:** Flip off if the consumer expects raw pointer-arithmetic rendering; on (default) is more readable.
- **Where / provenance:** P9/pointer-notation · ghidra-upstream · presentation-default · GH-558
- **Example:** `option arraynotation off`

### `truthycond` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** if (x != 0) where idiomatic C reads if (x); if (p == NULL) where if (!p) is wanted; explicit zero comparison in conditions unwanted; truthy condition rendering needs to match upstream ghidra for diffing.
- **What it does:** Render a boolean-context zero comparison in truthy form (if (x) / if (!p)) vs the explicit comparison (if (x != 0) / if (p == NULL)).
- **When to flip:** On by default (DIV-36): idiomatic C for if/while/for/ternary conditions and &&/||/! operands. Flip off to reproduce upstream Ghidra's explicit comparisons or to diff against Ghidra output. Float compares, enum-typed zeros, and equate-named zeros always keep the explicit form; value uses (v = (x != 0)) are never rewritten.
- **Where / provenance:** P9/condition-form · kuna · presentation-default · kuna-cnorm-fmt
- **Example:** `option truthycond off`

### `braceelide` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** if (x) { stmt; } where braceless if (x) stmt; is wanted; single-statement if body keeps braces; braced one-liner bodies unwanted; brace style needs to match upstream ghidra for diffing.
- **What it does:** Render a single-statement if body braceless with the statement indented on the next line (on) vs always braced (off).
- **When to flip:** On by default (DIV-37): idiomatic C for one-statement then-bodies. Flip off to reproduce upstream Ghidra's braced form or to diff against Ghidra output. Only plain single-statement bodies elide: labels, comments, and multi-statement bodies keep their braces; the if (cond) goto L; one-liner and else-if collapse are unaffected.
- **Where / provenance:** P9/brace-form · kuna · presentation-default · kuna-cnorm-fmt
- **Example:** `option braceelide off`

### `partialaccess` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** the emitted C contains a member named like `._4_2_` or `._0_8_`; a variable is read as `v1._6_1_` and the text does not compile; a 16-byte register pair returns as `v1._0_16_`; a libc record such as `stat` is read as `v3._24_4_`.
- **What it does:** Print a partial access of a variable that no member names as C instead of Ghidra's artificial `name._<off>_<size>_` member. `PrintC::pushPartialSymbol` (printc.cc:2106-2117) spells the bytes of a variable no field covers as `v1._4_2_` for the two bytes at offset 4 -- not C, so the text does not compile and a reader has to know the convention. With the option on, an access of a width C has a scalar for prints the way kuna already prints those bytes reached through a pointer: `((T *)&v1)[k]` when the offset is a multiple of the width (`k` is the offset divided by the width, IDA's `WORDn`/`BYTEn` reading), `*(T *)&v1` at offset 0, `*(T *)((char *)&v1 + off)` for an unaligned offset, `*(T *)&buf[off]` (and `*(T *)buf` at offset 0) for bytes taken out of a byte array, whose subscripts already count bytes, and `((char *)&v1)[off]` where the caller takes the address of a position inside the variable. `T` is the accessed value's own type when that is a scalar of exactly the access width, else the unknown type of that width (the float of that width when the access carries a float, which an integer `T` would convert); a 16-byte access on a 64-bit target reads through `unsigned __int128`, the GCC and Clang 16-byte integer. A view of a volatile access keeps the qualifier on its pointee (`*(volatile unsigned int *)cursor`), so it stays one access of its width. A sixteen-byte temporary whose type is only an inferred array of unknown bytes, which nothing but truncations, copies, merges and bitwise operations read and no load or array copy defines, is declared `unsigned __int128` instead of `char[16]`, so a whole-width value can be assigned to it. A member path in front of the token is kept (`((unsigned int *)&v1.flagfield)[1]`). Every form is an lvalue, so a partial store prints the same way, and the offset is the byte offset into the variable's storage exactly as in the token it replaces, so the reading is the target's memory order on every architecture. C has no scalar of 3, 5, 6, 7 or 9 to 15 bytes: a plain store or copy of such a width, or of 16 bytes, prints as `memset`/`memcpy` of exactly its bytes (`memset(&v11,0,0x10)`, `memcpy((char *)&v1 + 0x10,(char *)&d + 0x10,0x38)`), a whole array variable taking a copy out of such bytes the same way; a read of 3, 5, 6 or 7 bytes out of a scalar prints as the `SUB<in><out>(v,k)` intrinsic the output already uses for a truncation (`k` counted from the value's low end); any other access of such a width keeps Ghidra's token, which no compiler accepts, rather than a spelling that would compile to another value. No form is an array-typed value. C output only; the Rust printer keeps its own spelling. The forms reinterpret a variable through another type, as IDA's macros do, so recompiling the text wants `-fno-strict-aliasing` like any decompiler output that does.
- **When to flip:** On by default: the emitted C should be C, so a partial access no member names prints as a typed pointer access (`((short *)&v1)[2]`) instead of Ghidra's `v1._4_2_`. The XML datatest scripts that pin Ghidra's `._<off>_<size>_` spelling set it off (`Enum Reading #2`, `Stack Return #5`). Flip OFF to read Ghidra's notation, which is shorter and is what a Ghidra user expects, or to diff against Ghidra output.
- **Where / provenance:** P9/pointer-notation · kuna · presentation-default · kuna-partialaccess
- **Example:** `option partialaccess off`

### `rustarrayzero` -- on | off, default `off`

- **Symptoms:** Rust assigns scalar zero to a recovered [u8; 16] destination; a wide zero store fails with Rust E0308; a byte-array field needs a contextually typed zero value.
- **What it does:** Emit [0; N] for a Rust STORE of constant zero into a nonempty integer byte array when the value width, destination width and element count match exactly. Elements must have size and alignment one and cannot be enums. Preserve the destination expression and evaluation count without introducing a more strongly aligned scalar pointer. Nonzero values, other element types and inconsistent widths keep their previous handling; diagnostic cast suppression remains effective. C and Go output are unchanged.
- **When to flip:** Off in every preset. Enable when a recovered byte-array destination receives scalar zero and Rust rejects the assignment with E0308. The initial default-on build exceeded the 5% speed budget on a small C control: +5.075% CPU median across 64 balanced pairs, with -0.119% wall median. That C path does not call this helper, so the measurement is retained without a causal performance claim. The correction is opt-in under the speed policy.
- **Where / provenance:** P9/array-cover-width · kuna · correctness-fix · rust-zero-byte-array-store
- **Example:** `option rustarrayzero on`

### `bytearrayc` -- on | off, default `off`

- **Symptoms:** mapped unsigned char array uses invalid ._offset_size_ members; wide byte-array accesses need compilable C; unaligned mapped integer transfer needs an alias-safe C representation.
- **What it does:** Emit standard C byte-transfer helpers for direct nonvolatile integer accesses of 2, 4 or 8 bytes within a mapped global byte array. Helpers preserve target endianness, unaligned offsets and overlapping copies without wider pointer casts. One-byte accesses retain their subscript; whole-array integer covers use the same helpers. Other types, wider values and volatile annotations retain their existing rendering. Requires C11 and fixed-width integer types.
- **When to flip:** Opt in when recompiling mapped byte-array accesses that otherwise use artificial ._offset_size_ members. Off keeps the existing width-carrying notation. This does not supply a C representation for volatile wide accesses or vector/aggregate values.
- **Where / provenance:** P9/array-cover-width · kuna · presentation-default · mapped-byte-array-c
- **Example:** `option bytearrayc on`

### `globalref` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** a call argument is a raw address behind a cast, like sub_e4ca((struct_2 *)0x2b080); (unsigned long *)0x21180 or (void *)0x2b460 where IDA prints qword_21180 or &unk_2B460; getopt_long's option table prints as (option *)0x2a0c0; a loop runs from (int *)0x1a664 to (int *)0x1a690; the same global is dat_2b080 in one statement and (struct_2 *)0x2b080 in the next; a constant address you want to keep as an address (flip off).
- **What it does:** Print a pointer-typed constant that addresses program data as the address of the global it names, `&dat_<addr>`, instead of the forced-hex integer behind a cast, `(struct_2 *)0x2b080`. `PrintC::pushConstant`'s pointer arm has no other spelling for a constant `ActionConstantPtr` could not link to an existing global Symbol, and a stripped image has none for most of its data, so every address a declared or recovered pointer type reaches keeps a cast; the type campaign made that commoner, mostly through `protoorder` stating a callee's recovered parameter types to its callers (coreutils `ls` -O0 went from `sub_e4ca(0x2b080)` to `sub_e4ca((struct_2 *)0x2b080)`). When on, the function records the global as an object of the pointed-to type and the `decompile-project` header declares it (`extern struct_2 dat_2b080;`), so `&dat_2b080` has exactly the constant's pointer type and the cast is gone because the object is declared at that type; its value is the address it replaces wherever `dat_2b080` is placed at 0x2b080. The name is the one kuna already prints for an unnamed global it reads directly. Refused, keeping the cast: an address outside every loaded section the loader classifies as program data (code, TLS templates, `.got`/`.plt`/`.eh_frame`/`.dynamic`/`.interp`, the ELF loader tables, import slots, or no section at all -- a pointer-typed `0x1` or `-1` is not an address); an address a global Symbol already covers; a value the same function also reads as a number (an ordering compare, multiply, divide, remainder or shift on a non-pointer, the `inferfuncentry` BUFSIZ shape); an address the function uses at two different pointed-to types; storage the function also reads or writes directly at another start, width or type (a two-, four- or eight-byte `undefinedN` is accepted against the unsigned integer of its size, the C type every surface spells it as); a pointer to code; and a `void *` reader for which C's implicit conversion is not exactly the conversion the cast performed (an argument, a returned value, a copy or store into `void *` storage and an equality test against another `void *` are). An address the function only ever uses through `void *` is declared at the one type the function reads it at directly, or as the unknown byte. The header declares one type per address and never a scalar that disagrees with a direct `dat_<addr>` access anywhere in the program, which would silently change what that access computes: a record some function takes the address of wins (a scalar access of it does not compile), then the one type the direct accesses agree on, then the taken types by size and count; direct accesses at two types declare nothing and a comment says so. Other types are listed in a comment on the line.
- **When to flip:** On by default. Flip off to reproduce upstream Ghidra's (and kuna's pre-existing) `(T *)0x<addr>` spelling, or when a consumer greps the C for raw addresses. Measured over the 45-binary castbench corpus (coreutils fmt/ls/sort/du/cp/tail/wc, grep, gzip, diffutils, tar, find at O0/O2/O2-noinline): every one of the 1,883 changed lines is exactly the `(T *)0x<addr>` -> `&dat_<addr>` substitution, 1,979 casts removed (61% of the constant-address casts), no line added, removed or moved, and the output with the option off is byte-identical to the build without it. On the 4,815 functions kuna and IDA both emit, casts go 45,126 -> 44,001 (236.8 -> 230.9 per 1,000 lines, 1.193x -> 1.163x IDA); 486 functions have fewer casts and none more. Variables and types are untouched, so type_match cannot move (1,609 = 1,609 perfect on the 444-slice sweep). KNOWN LIMIT: a project header can hold one declaration per address. Over the 45 exports it declares 891 globals, 173 of them with another type listed in the comment (a record and the member at its start is the common case), where a body that used the other type now passes a pointer of the declared one -- a diagnosed incompatible-pointer warning, never a changed value; 60 addresses are left undeclared because the program reads them directly at two types. `gcc -fsyntax-only` over the 45 exports: 36,648 -> 36,471 errors, 14,962 -> 15,348 warnings.
- **Where / provenance:** P9/constant-address-global · ida · presentation-default · castcampaign-globalref
- **Example:** `option globalref off`

### `warnstyle` -- inline | banner, default `inline`

- **Symptoms:** full-line WARNING banner comments clutter the output; warning text wanted inline at the end of the statement it describes; terse warning slugs unwanted; full upstream warning text needed; warning style needs to match upstream ghidra for diffing.
- **What it does:** Render analysis warnings as terse end-of-line // slugs on the line they describe (inline) vs full /* WARNING: ... */ banner lines (banner).
- **When to flip:** Inline by default (DIV-38): usage(1); // no-return, if (v8) { // branch-flip, prototype-line // early-return x3. Flip to banner to reproduce upstream Ghidra's full warning text or to grep for the long-form messages. Unknown warning texts keep their full text behind a warn: marker; user/dwarf_lines comments always keep banner lines.
- **Where / provenance:** P9/warning-style · kuna · presentation-default · kuna-cnorm-fmt
- **Example:** `option warnstyle banner`

### `fpuemu` -- off | auto | on, default `auto`

- **Symptoms:** a DOS program's float code decompiles as calls through swi(0x35) and other INT 34h-3Dh vectors; Control flow encountered bad instruction data in a DOS function that does float math; a phantom function starts inside an INT 35h instruction's operand bytes; swi(0x3d) calls where the program waits for the coprocessor.
- **What it does:** Decode the 8087 emulator's software interrupts as the x87 instructions they stand for. A DOS program built by Microsoft's or Borland's compilers for the emulator carries no x87 opcodes: the linker's emulator fixups (FIDRQQ, FIWRQQ, FIERQQ and friends) turn each WAIT+ESC pair into INT 34h+n (ESC D8h+n) followed by the instruction's ModR/M and displacement, INT 3Ch followed by a byte holding the segment override (bits 6-7: DS, SS, CS, ES) and the ESC opcode, or INT 3Dh for FWAIT, and the emulator services them at run time. Read as plain x86 the operand bytes become garbage: CD 35 E8 (FLD1) is INT 35h and a near CALL that mints a phantom function, an FILD [bp-16h] swallows the following FWAIT into a far JMP, and the function ends in bad instruction data. x86-16.sla now keeps the ESC instructions in a table that also reads their emulated encodings wherever its context bit fpuEmu is 1, emitting the same p-code as the real instruction, so the C shows the float arithmetic. `auto` (the default) sets the bit on an MS-DOS executable whose load module holds emulator code: at least two emulated instructions that run straight into an emulated FWAIT or follow one, a pair a compiler emits at the end of every float sequence and data almost never holds (a table of INT n; RET thunks holds none). `on` sets it on any 16-bit x86 image, including a raw one; `off` keeps the interrupts.
- **When to flip:** Leave auto: a DOS program linked with the 8087 emulator decompiles its float code, and every other input (no fpuEmu bit outside x86-16.sla, no emulator code in the image) is byte-identical. Use on for a raw-image or .COM program that uses the emulator but has too little float code for the evidence, off to read the interrupts as the bytes encode them.
- **Where / provenance:** P2/decode-context · kuna · correctness-fix · kuna-1288-fpuemu
- **Example:** `kuna decompile-all dazzle.exe --option fpuemu off`

### `arrayextent` -- off | bound | on, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** a stack array is declared with 4 elements while a loop subscripts it further; the elements after the fourth of a local array are separate scalars that are assigned and never read; a recompiled function reads past a local array under AddressSanitizer; a masked or clamped index (`v[n & 7]`, `min(n, 5)`) subscripts a smaller declared array.
- **What it does:** Size an indexed stack array past the four elements upstream assumes when its guard has no locked range. `bound`: an indexed base whose pointer is the stack base plus constants plus indices bounded by their known bits (`v[n & 7]`), and which is only dereferenced, gets room for every element those LOADs and STOREs may touch, up to the next pointer base above it; every slot of the element width inside that reach joins the array, whether the function reads it on its own or not. `on` adds: an indexed base with no such bound, or a guard with a step but no locked range, takes each following slot of its element size while the slot is contiguous with its elements, holds only unlocked fixed hints of that width whose type keeps the element type, starts no other open range, and is observed only through a pointer (no direct read of the slot, and no other use of a value copied into it except copies into stack slots outside the array); a constant stored into the last slot it takes no longer lets upstream's constant absorption grow the array past it, unless upstream's merge of the same hints, with the array at its old length, reaches past that slot anyway. `off` is upstream's [0,3] floor.
- **When to flip:** On by default (0/675 datatest assertions move). With it OFF a local array that a loop indexes up to a clamped bound (`for (i = 0; i < n && i < 6; i++) t += v[i];`, `v[n & 7]`) is declared with four elements and the rest split into scalars that are assigned and never read, so the printed loop subscripts past the declared array and the C reads the wrong object (ASan reports a stack-buffer-overflow on the recompiled function). `bound` keeps only the sound known-bits sizing. Flip `bound` or `off` to see the upstream split for a bisect.
- **Where / provenance:** P6/stack-frame-layout · kuna · correctness-fix · GH-867
- **Example:** `option arrayextent off`

### `arraystride` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** loop walks an array with a raw offset accumulator (iVar += 0x414) instead of an index; strided induction offset never re-expressed as counter*stride array indexing.
- **What it does:** Re-express a strength-reduced array walk: rewrite a loop offset accumulator (acc += sizeof) as counter*stride so the array index is recovered.
- **When to flip:** A strided loop renders a raw offset accumulator (e.g. iVar += 0x414) instead of an index. On by default (DIV-3); flip off to restore the upstream accumulator rendering.
- **Where / provenance:** P3/simplification-quiescence · ghidra-upstream · structure-recovery · GH-8724
- **Example:** `option arraystride on`

### `rustabi` -- off | auto | always, default `auto`

- **Symptoms:** a Rust Result or Option producer recovers as bool and the payload register is missing from the return; a local commented with a register name is declared and read but never assigned anywhere in the function; a call to a Rust function that returns Result renders with no output at all; a discriminant guard tests a variable whose companion payload variable has no definition; two-register return recovered as one register when the first half holds a setCC flag.
- **What it does:** On a rustc-built image, keep the two-register value a ScalarPair return (Result, Option, a slice, a fat pointer) is carried in, and connect it at the call. kuna already RECOVERS the pair -- the x86-64 cspec join_dual_class output rule matches the RAX/RDX trials and buildReturnOutput builds the join -- and then loses it twice. On the producer, SubvariableFlow::tryReturnPull truncates the RETURN to the logical width of the value it is tracing; rustc materializes the discriminant with `xor %eax,%eax; setb %al`, so RAX is a ONE-BIT logical value and the whole return narrows to it, deleting the other register: `Result<u32,u32>` comes back as `bool prod(uint4 a0)` with the EDX payload gone. On the consumer, FuncCallSpecs::buildOutputFromTrials handles one used output trial and returns early on two, so the call gets NO output at all and every read of the payload register renders as a local the function never assigns -- the phantom `int4 v3; // edx` that a Result guard tests. The two seams get DIFFERENT classifications, because they do not see the same thing. At the producer the concatenation's halves are values the function computed, so classify_return_pair reads their shape (never a size: size does not predict rustc's choice -- `Result<u32,u32>` is 8 bytes and a pair, `Result<Box<u64>,u32>` is 16 bytes and goes through memory). A pair is recognized when the least-significant half is discriminant-shaped -- a value whose known non-zero bits fit in a byte, which covers both the branchy `mov $0/$1` tag and the branchless `setCC` one -- and vetoed when that half traces back to the function's own incoming pointer argument, which is the sret epilogue rather than a tag. At the CALL there are no callee values in the IR at all (both halves are INDIRECT creations), so classify_call_output_pair rests on the model rule that matched, on the caller reading both halves out of the call, and on a bounded decode of the resolved callee: when that decode covers every path to a RETURN and never writes the payload register, the caller's read is a clobber and the pair is REFUSED. That callee check is one-sided -- it can refute a pair, never confirm one -- so `ScalarPair` at the consumer means `no counter-example`, not `the callee returns a pair`. At `auto` the rules act only on an image the loader detected as rustc-produced; at `always` the language test is dropped.
- **When to flip:** On (`auto`) by default: a Rust binary's `Result`/`Option` payload survives - the producer no longer recovers as `bool` when the disassembly plainly writes a second return register, and a consumer testing `v & 1` no longer reads a companion local that is declared, read, and never assigned. Measured on a 4.9 MB static-PIE rustc binary (4194 functions): phantom guards -- conditional guards whose condition reads a local the function never assigns -- fall from 1476 of 9026 to 1116 of 9039 (-24.4%), never-assigned locals from 4805 to 3533 (-26.5%), and the functions containing one from 1225 to 983; 408 functions change (392 with strictly fewer phantoms, 1 with one more), every inspected one gaining a payload variable or a call output (`&str` fat pointers out of `String::borrow`, the `(usize, usize)` out of `physical_core_count`, `Instant::now`). Zero functions change across grep/sort/faillog/libselinux and the betaflight ARM fixture, because `auto` cannot see a non-Rust image, and `/usr/bin/ncat` and `/usr/bin/htop` are likewise byte-identical off vs auto. The call seam's callee veto costs nothing measurable on that corpus -- the whole-binary output is byte-identical with the veto ablated -- because a real ScalarPair producer does write its payload register; what it refuses is the caller that reads a register its callee provably never sets. Speed on that same Rust binary, interleaved off/auto, minimum of 6: 169.04 s -> 169.37 s, **+0.20%** (budget 5%); two separate min-of-3 runs disagreed in sign (+0.38% and -0.78%), so the real cost is below this machine's measurement floor. The classification is deliberately narrow (one discriminant byte, one payload register) and the pair it keeps alive is rendered as a raw `undefined16`/`[u8; 16]` container until a later pass gives it an enum type, so a producer that used to render as a tidy `bool` now renders as a two-field aggregate -- more information, less polish. `auto` cannot touch a non-Rust image at all (the language fact comes from the analyzer tier, which the XML datatest bootstrap never runs), so the change is confined to Rust output; use `always` to force the rules on a corpus with no `.comment` record, such as a stage-test bytechunk, and `off` to restore the one-register rendering.
- **Where / provenance:** P4/output-prototype · kuna · correctness-fix · kuna-rust-scalarpair-return
- **Example:** `option rustabi auto`

### `argclobber` -- on | off, default `on` (destructive opt-in)

- **Symptoms:** a call passes one more argument than the callee's own recovered prototype takes; the last argument of a call is a local that is never assigned anywhere in the function; a declaration carries a // rdx storage comment and no write; two calls to the same callee in one function render with different arities and the longer one reads an undefined value; Ghidra names the same value extraout_RDX and kuna renders it as an ordinary local.
- **What it does:** Drop the TRAILING register argument of a call when nothing on the caller's side put a value in that register. Heritage::guardCalls (heritage.cc:1444) plants an INDIRECT *creation* for every killed-by-call register that is also a possible OUTPUT location of the callee's model -- rdx is one on x86-64, because a 16-byte value returns in rax:rdx -- and AncestorRealistic::enterNode (funcdata_varnode.cc:2043) answers pop_success for exactly that op, recording ParamTrial::setIndCreateFormed on the way. With onlyOpUse satisfied the trial is active and ParamListStandard::fillinMap marks it used, so a register the caller never wrote for this call becomes its last argument, and the local it reads is assigned nowhere: coreutils fmt -O2 renders `v12 = sub_3700(stdin,"-",v10);` with `unsigned long v9; // rdx` and `unsigned long v11; // rdx` never written, against a DWARF prototype of two parameters, while the other two sites of the same callee render one and two arguments. Upstream reads the same bit back on the RETURN side only -- ParamListStandardOut::fillinMap (fspec.cc:1721) scores a remainder-formed or indirect-creation-formed trial no-use when its ParamEntry is not first in its class -- and the input list has no such test, so the evidence that disqualifies a return value is ignored for an argument (stock Ghidra emits the same three-argument call and names the phantom extraout_RDX). This option applies that sentence to the input list, bounded by eight clauses. The trial must be a REGISTER trial carrying isIndCreateFormed, which is the upstream return-side test applied to the input list. The clobber must reach the call DIRECTLY: the trial's defining op is the indirect creation, or a MULTIEQUAL one of whose immediate inputs is one -- tar's str_days(pc,buffer,n) is called with n live from a dominating block and a clobber merging in behind a second phi, and that argument is real. Every one of those creations must be a creation of THE ARGUMENT REGISTER ITSELF: the first return register of every ABI is also killed-by-call and a possible output location, so a preceding call's result is an indirect creation too until the output seam resolves it, and a value the caller MOVED into an argument register is a value the caller is passing -- u-boot -O2 sub_60827fa4 carries ofnode_read_u32_default(dev->node,"bus-width",1) from r0 into r3 through a pair of predicated movs and prints it with %u. EVERY OTHER INPUT OF THAT JOIN must be a division by-product: the value an idiv leaves in the remainder register while the caller uses only the quotient, reached through a SUBPIECE of the low half, a zero or sign extension or a constant mask and nothing else. One clobber among a phi's inputs says nothing about the other paths, so each has to be positively classified as a value nobody placed either, and upstream scores a remainder-formed piece exactly like an indirect-creation-formed one on the return side. Without this clause a caller that forwards its own second parameter on the non-clobber path (`mov %r12,%rdx`) loses both the argument and the parameter, and `void caller(long,unsigned long)` renders as `void caller(long)`. The CALLEE's own RECOVERED PROTOTYPE must exist and must have no parameter overlapping those bytes. This is the clause the rule rests on and the reason it can be a default: nothing on the caller's side can say whether the callee wanted the register, and the parameter list kuna gets from decompiling that function can. protoorder states it for every callee it decompiles before the caller, and states nothing for a callee inside a recursive component, one with no recovered body such as a PLT import, one that recovered no parameters at all, and one whose prototype is already declared -- so "nothing stated" and "cannot tell" are the same answer and both decline. The recovered list must also ACCOUNT for every argument the drop leaves behind, storage for storage: a recovery short of what the call passes is not a statement that the tail is unwanted but a statement that the recovery did not reach the tail, and a forwarding thunk (mov (%rdi),%rax; jmp *%rax) is exactly that shape -- it recovers one parameter while the function it tail calls consumes three. protoorder does NOT decline a variadic callee: its under-recovery and register-file guards belong to the lock mode, the declared-... decline cannot fire on a stripped image, and a stripped SysV variadic is STATED (long vlog(int,long,...) built with gcc -O2 states three parameters).
