The callee must write that register itself or through what it calls (gcc's IPA-RA lets a caller keep its own value there across a callee that never touches it, so such a read proves nothing), must start a symbol of the image's own symbol table and reach a RETURN; a register-window function counts only writes of the register its `restore` moves into the second one, and one whose first instruction stores the second register (`push {r0-r3,lr}`) proves nothing. The call sites come from one scan of the executable bytes for direct-call encodings (PowerPC `bl`, MIPS `jal`/`bal`, SPARC `call`, ARM and Thumb `bl`/`blx`) whose target starts a symbol, and MIPS PIC `jalr $25` calls whose `$25` a GOT load gave (the entry read at the GOT pointer the caller's prologue computes), each decoded again before it is read; a MIPS `lwl`/`lwr` pair into the second register writes it without reading it; and the walk after a call keeps on each path what its branches decided about the flags (ARM's `ldrne r1,..; orrnes r2,r1,r0` reads no stale `r1`); the verdict is the least fixed point over the functions it reaches (up to 32 functions and 48 call sites; a caller reached only by handing the pair back is judged by its own callers), from facts cached per image, so every run mode prints the same, and an image without symbols proves nothing this way. A declared, DWARF or `--assert prototype` 8-byte return is placed by the model in the ABI's order in every mode. `on` is the instruction-shape guess: the ABI's order when the second register's value looks returned on purpose at every live RETURN (kuna_bejoin::join_order), which also reads such an `int` as the `long long` it matches. `off` joins every pair first register low, as upstream does.
- **When to flip:** Leave at `callers` (the default): it changes a big-endian or AVR pair only on proof, from the function's own instructions or from how its callers read it, so an `int` keeps its first-register reading, and a function and its callers agree however they are decompiled. Set `evidence` to judge each function from its own instructions alone. Set `on` when a big-endian function's 64-bit return or call result still prints with its halves swapped (`CONCAT44(low,high)`) and its disassembly shows a genuine 64-bit value (a 64-bit sum or difference, an ARM `umull` or SPARC `umul` product, a value an unproven callee returns): `on` reads those in the ABI's order too, and also reads an `int` worked out from the high half of a 64-bit temporary as that `long long` -- `int sum_hi(u64 a,u64 b){return (a+b)>>32;}` on PowerPC -O2, `((u64)a*b)>>32` and `a / 641` on ARM big-endian, MIPS gcc -O0's `>> 32` -- so check such a function against the disassembly. Better still, `--assert prototype` the 8-byte return, which joins it right in every mode. `off` gives upstream's first-register-low join everywhere. Little-endian targets other than AVR never reach the option. Measured with the default against off: over 698 big-endian objects (bash, cronie, diffutils, dpkg, findutils, grep, kmod, libbsd, libedit, Lua, openssh, shadow and sysvinit for PowerPC, SPARC and ARM big-endian with clang and MIPS with gcc at -O0 and -O2), SQLite and zlib for the same four targets, and every shape GH-904 lists built at -O0 to -O3 and -Os with callers before and after their callees, decompiled whole, narrowed, with `--jobs 2` and one at a time, no function whose DWARF or source return type is narrower than 8 bytes changes (the memory and call-pair shapes added later change 37 64-bit returns and 6 of their callers among 20,759 functions of that corpus and none narrower; of the authored shapes only a volatile 64-bit read's high word moves); compiling the printed C of those shapes against their source, functions go from wrong to right and none from right to wrong. Little-endian x86-64, i386, ARM, AArch64, MIPSel, PowerPC LE and RISC-V output is byte-identical. `callers` against `evidence`: every function it newly proves over those 813 objects, the four SQLite builds and 1,428 authored objects (1,570) returns eight bytes by its DWARF or source type, as do the 75 it proves in two static PowerPC SQLite shells linked with glibc (by DWARF, or libgcc's and glibc's 64-bit routines), and no function's return changes width; 250 functions of the corpus and those of SQLite now return or read a 64-bit value high word first; over 16 gcc MIPS PIC shared objects (SQLite, Lua, zlib, authored shapes) the 47 functions the GOT calls newly prove return eight bytes by DWARF, and three `int`/`void` SQLite functions an unaligned `lwl`/`lwr` load had proven no longer are. A pair a caller passes straight on as the next call's arguments (`bl f; bl use64`), or that no caller reads the second word of, stays as `evidence` prints it.
- **Where / provenance:** P4/output-prototype · kuna · correctness-fix · bejoin
- **Example:** `option bejoin callers`

### `bejoinpass` -- off | whole | high, default `whole`

- **Symptoms:** a big-endian function that returns a call's long long prints CONCAT44((int)v1,(int)(v1 >> 0x20)); a wrapper of a 64-bit callee on PowerPC or MIPS returns the callee's value with its halves swapped; a u32 that returns the high word of a 64-bit call result prints as unsigned long long.
- **What it does:** Join a big-endian register pair that a call hands back and the function returns untouched as one value. `bejoin` decides a function's returned pair by that function's own proof and a call's output pair by its callee's, so a pair passing from one to the other unchanged was judged twice and could join in both orders at once: a wrapper with no proof of its own of a proven 64-bit callee (`jal add64; nop; lw $31,..; jr $31` on MIPS o32, `bl add64; ..; blr` on PowerPC, which `passthrough`'s tail-return claim gives the callee's two registers) joined its RETURN first register low while the call read the pair high word first, and printed `CONCAT44((int)v1,(int)(v1 >> 0x20))`, the callee's value with its halves swapped; a function proven by its callers or declared 8 bytes that returns what an unknown callee left in the pair (a MIPS PIC call through the GOT, a call through a function pointer, a PowerPC tail call into an unproven callee) printed the same swap the other way round. A side with a proof now fixes the order of both: a call whose two registers reach, untouched through moves and phis, the high and low words of a RETURN joined high word first joins high word first too, which changes only how the same bits print (`v1 = (*hook)(); ext(); return v1;`, kuna_bejoinpass::call_order). A function with no proof of its own whose every live RETURN hands back the pair a call to a proven callee left there untouched (kuna_bejoinpass::settle_return) has the bytes of both `u64 w(){return add64(..);}` and `u32 hi(){return add64(..) >> 32;}`, and nothing in it tells the two apart: `whole` (the default) returns the callee's whole value high word first, `return add64(..);`, right for the wrapper and too wide for `hi`; `high` returns its first register alone, the callee's high word, `return (int)((unsigned long long)add64(..) >> 0x20);`, right for `hi` and too narrow for the wrapper; under `whole` too, a RETURN whose first register went through more moves than its second (gcc -O0's `(u32)(v >> 32)`, `mov r3,r0; mov r0,r3` after the pair is moved back) keeps the first register alone. A caller reading the second register (`bejoin callers`) or a declared, DWARF or `--assert prototype` 8-byte return proves the function and keeps the pair whole in either mode. The function's own verdict stays unproven, so under `whole` a caller in the image that reads only its first register (a sign test, `if (w() < 0)`) still reads that register as the low word, `(int)w()`. `off` leaves each side to its own verdict. Only pairs of two 4-byte registers (PowerPC r3:r4, MIPS o32 v0:v1, SPARC o0:o1, ARM big-endian r0:r1) under `bejoin evidence` or `callers` are judged; every other target and mode is unchanged.
- **When to flip:** Leave at `whole` (the default): a pair handed back untouched prints as one value, and a function with no proof of its own that returns a proven 64-bit callee's pair returns the callee's value. Set `high` when such a function's source returns only the high word (`u32 hi(){return add64(..) >> 32;}`, or the first member of a struct a PowerPC `-msvr4-struct-return` callee returns in r3:r4), or when a caller in the image tests only its first register and prints `(int)w()` for what is the high word; better still, `--assert prototype` its true return, which every caller then reads. `off` restores the two separate verdicts and the swapped `CONCAT44((int)v1,(int)(v1 >> 0x20))`. Measured against `off` over 359 MIPS images (gcc and clang, -O0 to -O3 and -Os; zlib, Lua, SQLite and authored shapes; big- and little-endian PIC shared objects and big-endian objects) and 250 PowerPC images (gcc 13 and clang 14, the same sources, PIC and non-PIC) with their DWARF stripped: functions printing the swapped `CONCAT44((int)v,(int)(v >> 0x20))` fall from 22 to 4 on MIPS (the rest join a 64-bit temporary of the function's own, or a call's pair the function keeps rather than returns) and from 16 to 0 on PowerPC. Every function `whole` and `high` print differently is a wrapper with no proof of its own and an 8-byte DWARF return: 22 there (`i64 p8(int x){return fw(x);}`, `u64 ret_g(u64 a){return add64(a,3);}`) and 13 in compiler-rt's builtins and 64 SDL3 sources built for MIPS and PowerPC (clang 14, gcc 12 and 13, -O0 to -Os, PIC and non-PIC, soft-float; `SDL_TellIO`, the `SDL_IOStream` size and seek callbacks, soft-float `__floatdidf`). `whole` prints all 35 at their DWARF width, `high` none, and no `u32 hi()` shape occurs in any of these images; over big-endian MIPS and PowerPC glibc, libm, libgcc_s, libatomic, libgomp, libstdc++ and ld.so (Debian 12, Ubuntu 24.04) and angr's MIPS and PowerPC test binaries, 59 images and 30,677 functions, the two print byte-identically. Every other change prints a proven function's call pair high word first. x86-64, i386, little-endian ARM and MIPS, AArch64 and PowerPC64 LE output is byte-identical, as are 51 ARM big-endian objects.
- **Where / provenance:** P4/output-prototype · kuna · correctness-fix · bejoin
- **Example:** `option bejoinpass whole`

### `narrowext` -- off | abi | compiler, default `abi`

- **Symptoms:** a call to a function returning int is printed (unsigned long)(unsigned int)f() on RISC-V or LoongArch; a signed char or short result is zero-extended where the callee sign-extends it; a declared int parameter used as a 64-bit value prints (unsigned long)(unsigned int)x; a narrow result or parameter prints as CONCAT31(v1,f()) or CONCAT44(v1,x) with an unassigned v1.
- **What it does:** Extend a declared integer argument or return value narrower than its register as the calling convention does. A compiler spec states one extension per register entry (`zero`, `sign`, `inttype` or none), which cannot express what the RISC-V and LoongArch procedure-call standards say: an integer narrower than 32 bits is widened by the sign of its type, and a 32-bit one is then sign-extended to a 64-bit register whatever its sign. The RISC-V specs state `zero` and the LoongArch ones nothing, so a call to `int fi(int)` read as a 64-bit value printed `(unsigned long)(unsigned int)fi(k)`, and a callee that uses its `int` parameter as a 64-bit value printed `(unsigned long)(unsigned int)x`. The rule replaces the spec's extension at the two places it is applied: after a call whose return value is locked or committed narrower than the register (`ActionFuncLink::funcLinkOutput`, `FuncCallSpecs::commitNewOutputs`), and at the entry of a function whose parameter is locked narrower than its register (`ActionPrototypeTypes::extendInput`). Only a register entry, and only a value whose type states its sign (`int`, `unsigned`, `bool`, an enum) takes it: plain `char`, whose sign is the platform's while kuna's `char` is signed everywhere, an undefined type, a pointer, a float and a structure keep the spec's extension. A typed indirect call whose return value the rule extends is forced as declared instead of being left to recovery. `abi` applies each rule an ABI document states: RISC-V and LoongArch arguments and return values, the arguments of MIPS o32, n32 and n64 (System V MIPS supplement, SGI n32/n64 handbook) and the arguments of Apple arm64, which the caller extends to 32 bits. `compiler` adds what GCC and LLVM do where those documents are silent: a MIPS return value (and an EABI or o64 argument) is widened the same way, and an Apple arm64 return value narrower than 32 bits is widened to 32 bits by the callee, the bits above left unspecified; an x86-64 System V argument narrower than 32 bits is widened to 32 bits by the sign of its type, which GCC and clang callers do and clang callees rely on although the psABI does not say so. `off` keeps the spec's extension everywhere.
- **When to flip:** On by default (`abi`). Set `compiler` for a clang-built x86-64 binary whose functions read a declared `unsigned char`, `short` or `bool` parameter as a 32-bit value, which prints as `CONCAT31(v1,c)` with an unassigned `v1`, or for a MIPS or Apple arm64 binary whose callers read a narrow result as a whole register, which prints as `CONCAT31(v1,fc(k))` with an unassigned `v1` on MIPS or `(unsigned int)(unsigned char)esc(k)` on Apple arm64: every GCC and LLVM callee extends the value and every caller relies on it, but no ABI document says so, so it is not the default. Set `off` to get the compiler spec's extension back, for example when comparing with Ghidra. A narrow value the code compares or computes with as a whole register prints the extension it performs, `(long)k`, where the spec's zero extension folded away.
- **Where / provenance:** P4/output-prototype · kuna · correctness-fix · gh-816
- **Example:** `option narrowext compiler`

### `armfloatreturn` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** a double return becomes SUB84 or zero; an ARM hard-float function loses its d0 parameter; a caller reads an undefined floating result.
- **What it does:** On an ARM ELF whose container states the VFP procedure-call standard, recover complete scalar VFP return values and the double-width argument storage they use.
- **When to flip:** On by default: ARM hard-float code returns its double whole in d0 instead of truncating it to the low word, and keeps a double input. Requires consistent ELF ABI evidence (`Tag_ABI_VFP_args` or `EF_ARM_ABI_FLOAT_HARD`); soft-float, softfp, missing metadata, and explicit prototypes keep their existing contracts, so on any other image the option changes nothing. A double argument at a call needs the callee's declared or protoorder-recovered prototype, so it appears in a callee-first decompile-all, not in a single-function decompile. A returned constant no float literal spells (a NaN payload) is returned bit-exact through a union; AEABI and libgcc soft-float helpers keep the base standard; a VFP register-bank save or restore is no parameter and no result. Flip off to see the base-standard truncated return.
- **Where / provenance:** P4/output-prototype · kuna · correctness-fix · arm-hard-float-return
- **Example:** `option armfloatreturn on`

### `armfloatargs` -- on | off, default `on`

- **Symptoms:** missing floating argument; double input split into two words; caller and callee disagree on mixed argument contract.
- **What it does:** On an ARM ELF whose container states the VFP procedure-call standard, recover scalar hard-float inputs with their full floating widths and consistent caller/callee storage, on top of armfloatreturn. Uses positive VFP ABI evidence, preserves declared prototypes, keeps input widths independent of overlapping return storage, leaves the AAPCS-VFP back-fill slot out of recovered parameter lists, and gives a call the VFP inputs its callee's arity-sound contract states, a stated double held as two words passed whole; an unused trailing float an -O0 callee only spills is still passed though the callee's list omits it. Unknown cross-bank source order uses the model order; floating aggregates and vectors are recovered only as the scalar words or doubles their reads show, never as the source grouping.
- **When to flip:** On by default together with armfloatreturn (alone it changes nothing): scalar ARM VFP inputs keep their widths instead of disappearing, splitting into word parameters, or disagreeing with their callers. Unknown calls need a proven callee contract. Declared prototypes outrank recovery. Variadic format calls use base AAPCS storage. A double a callee reads only as integer words, as on single-precision FPUs, keeps what armfloatreturn recovers. Inert on every image without hard-float ABI evidence. Flip off to keep the base-standard word parameters.
- **Where / provenance:** P4/input-prototype · kuna · correctness-fix · arm-mixed-vfp-arguments
- **Example:** `option armfloatargs on`

### `infloopstyle` -- while | do, default `while`

- **Symptoms:** unconditional loop prints do-while (true) at the bottom; prefer while (true) at the top; need the previous infinite-loop spelling for comparison.
- **What it does:** Spell unconditional C loops as while (true) at the top or do-while (true) at the bottom.
- **When to flip:** While by default: unconditional loops print while (true) at the top. Set do to recover the previous spelling. Conditional do-while loops and Rust loop syntax keep their existing form.
- **Where / provenance:** P9/infinite-loop-style · kuna · presentation-default · server-infinite-loop-style
- **Example:** `option infloopstyle do`

### `armconstshift` -- on | off, default `off`

- **Symptoms:** a signed ARM value is shifted left by a constant in the emitted C; UBSan reports a left shift of a negative value in recompiled ARM output; a signed ARM shift overflows into the sign bit in recompiled output.
- **What it does:** Print a fixed 32-bit ARM LSL of a signed operand as a shift of its unsigned conversion, `(int)((unsigned int)x << n)`, so the emitted C is defined for negative values and for bits shifted into or past the sign. The shiftee is converted once, the signed result type is restored only when the p-code output is signed, unsigned and register-count shifts are unchanged, and a signed variable is never shifted in place.
- **When to flip:** Turn on when the emitted C must be free of signed-shift undefined behavior, e.g. before recompiling it with sanitizers or comparing it against the binary. Off by default because the conversion adds a cast pair to every ARM sign-bit test such as `x << 0x18 < 0`, which firmware uses for nearly every register flag check.
- **Where / provenance:** P9/cast-policy · kuna · correctness-fix · arm-fixed-signed-lsl
- **Example:** `option armconstshift on`

### `readonlycalls` -- off | on | <n>, default `65536`

- **Symptoms:** a function that reads many constant globals between calls exhausts memory during heritage; decompile of a huge function is killed before the first jump table is recovered; thousands of INDIRECTs over read-only globals survive in a large function's IR; a function prints read-only literals differently once it grows past the readonlycalls threshold.
- **What it does:** In a heritage pass that would guard at least N read-only-range and call pairs (default 65,536), give a call no INDIRECT guard over a read-only memory range the function never writes. A callee cannot change memory the image maps without write permission, so every read of such a range sees the value it had at entry and needs no definition per call. Upstream guards the range at every call with an unknown effect anyway: one INDIRECT per read-only global per call, plus the MULTIEQUALs their writes force at every join, and on a persistent range they survive dead-code removal; a large function that reads thousands of constants through thousands of calls builds millions of them. The count is the pass's calls times its new, read, read-only ranges in the default data space; below it every call keeps upstream's guard, whose chain the printer uses as a barrier (it keeps a copy of a read-only literal split per element, and an expression over a constant global from being printed again after a call), so the same function can print differently on either side of N. `on` leaves read-only ranges unguarded in every pass with a call, and `off` keeps every guard. A read-only range the function itself writes keeps its guards, as does any range whose read-only property is unknown.
- **When to flip:** On by default at 65,536 guards, the size at which the guards cost a huge function gigabytes. Set `on` to print every function as one above the threshold prints (no per-element copies of read-only literals, constant globals read again after calls), a smaller N to lower the size at which that starts, a larger N or `off` to keep upstream's guards in larger functions, for example to compare the SSA heritage builds for a large constant table read across calls.
- **Where / provenance:** P3/call-guard · kuna · performance · gh-1034
- **Example:** `option readonlycalls off`

### `persistcalls` -- off | on | <n>, default `65536`

- **Symptoms:** a function that touches thousands of globals between thousands of calls takes gigabytes and minutes to decompile; heritage builds millions of INDIRECTs over writable globals that survive dead-code removal; a huge initializer or finalizer exhausts memory in assignhigh or merging.
- **What it does:** In a heritage pass that would guard at least N persistent-RAM-range and call pairs (default 65,536), give a call an INDIRECT guard over a writable persistent global only where skipping it could show: a write reaches the call with no call in between; a read follows it, or reaches it, with no call or full write in between (reads are free reads, partial writes, returns, and every LOAD and STORE in the space, which can fold into direct accesses later); some path after it meets a full write, a STORE or the end before a read or kept guard, so the global stays live over the same code for merging; or a join of the global would otherwise take, on an edge in, the value from before it. Upstream guards every persistent global at every call whose effect on it is unknown, and the guards survive dead-code removal, so a function that touches thousands of globals across thousands of calls builds millions of them. A skipped call leaves the value from before it standing for the value after it, which these rules confine to the inputs of kept guards; a system call that guards memory counts as a STORE. A range a pass revisits keeps every guard; a later read or partial write that would cross a call left unguarded, a Varnode reaching past such a range, a join that still takes a stale value once every guard is built, the removal of a guard a read depends on, or a merge copy or removal of a guard whose input crosses a call left unguarded (it would store the value from before that call after it) restarts the function with every guard built, and the pass run once the re-flow budget is spent keeps every guard. A skipped guard, and a join only skipped guards needed, keep their op and Varnode numbers. Below N every call keeps upstream's guard, and jump-table recovery partials always do. The count is the pass's calls times its new ranges in the default data space.
- **When to flip:** On by default at 65,536 guards, the size at which the guards cost a huge function gigabytes and minutes. Set `on` to place the sparse guards in every pass with a call, a larger N or `off` to keep upstream's guard on every persistent global at every call, for example to compare heritage's IR with upstream.
- **Where / provenance:** P3/call-guard · kuna · performance · gh-1034
- **Example:** `option persistcalls off`

## Programmatic use

```bash
# discover (machine-readable; includes tier + symptoms):
kuna catalog --json

# transforms only:
kuna catalog --tier transform

# decompile with an option flipped (repeatable):
kuna decompile ./a.out main --option gotoreduce off
kuna decompile ./sparc.elf main --option returnpair single
```
